entry.title: Math for AI 105 Warm-up
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on TA. Vo Huynh Quang Nguyen’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read Math for AI 104 or been familiar with probability and statistics. Note that only basic probability material is introduced here; we’ll pick up specific concepts when in need.

In today’s post, we’ll explore basic probability concepts: random variables, probability distribution, and descriptive statistics.

Random Variable (RV)

Definition

Let’s use some kid-friendly scenarios to introduce the idea of a random variable.

Random Experiment Random Variable Description
Picking a candy from a jar The candy color If you get red, X = Red.
If you get green, X = Green.
Spinning a wheel at a fair The number of tickets you win If it lands on “10 tickets”, X = 10.
If it lands on “good luck next time”, X = 0.
An entire soccer match The number of goals If the final score is 2-1, X = 3.
Throwing a dart The distance from the landing to the bullseye If you hit close, X might be 0.5 inch.
If you miss badly, X might be 5 inches.
Throwing a dart three times The number of times the dart lands within 2 inches from the bullseye If you land within the range once, X = 1.
If you lands outside of the range once, X = 4.


From above cases, we can think of a random variable as a real number depending on the outcome of a random experiment.

Formally, a random variable $X$ is a function $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, $s \mapsto X(s)$ where $\Omega$ is the sample space—set of outcomes and $\mathbb{R}$ is the set of real numbers. Let’s delve into two types of random variables and their examples to nail this concept.

Discrete RV - Probability

A discrete random variable $X$ is a function $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ where $\Omega$ is a finite or countably infinite set. Since the range of this function contains numbers representing mutually exclusive events, we can measure probability on random variables and the sum of all those probabilities must be 1.

Probability on random variables are known as probability distribution. Probability mass and density are common probability distributions.

Probability Mass Function (PMF), denoted by $p(x)$ or $p_X(x)$, measures the probabiltiy of possible values of a random variable, that is, $p(x) = p_X(x) = P(X = x)$.

Cummulative Distribution Function (CDF), denoted by $F(x)$ or $F_X(x)$, is the cumulative probability of of all possible values less than equal to a specific number, that is, $F_X(x) = P(X \le x)$.

We’ll see examples demonstrated in two following tables.

Concept Description/Meaning Result
Experiment Toss a fair coin 3 times in a roll Each time has 2 possible outcomes including head and tail
Sample Space H is a head and T is a tail $\Omega = \\\{HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT\\\}$
$n(\Omega) = 2^3 = 8$
Random Variable The number of heads in the sequence $X(s) \in \\\{0, 1, 2, 3\\\}$
  • $X(s) = 2 \Rightarrow s \in \\\{\text{HHT, HTH, THH}\\\} \Rightarrow n(X(s)) = 3$
  • $X(s) = 0 \Rightarrow s \in \\\{\text{TTT}\\\} \Rightarrow n(X(s)) = 0$
  • $1 < X(s) \le 3 \Rightarrow s \in \\\{\text{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH}\\\} \Rightarrow n(X(s)) = 4$
The index of the first head (0 if there is no head) $X(s) \in \\\{0, 1, 2, 3\\\}$
  • $s = TTT \Rightarrow X(s) = 0$
  • $s = TTH \Rightarrow X(s) = 3$
  • $s = HTH \Rightarrow X(s) = 1$


Below, consider the number of heads in the sequence as a random variable.

Random Variables PMF CDF
$X(s) = 2 \Rightarrow P(X = 2) = \frac{3}{8}$ $p(2) = \frac{3}{8}$ :x:
$1 < X(s) \le 3 \Rightarrow P(1 < X \le 3) = \frac{4}{8}$ :x: :x:
$X(s) \le 2 \Rightarrow X \in \\\{0, 1, 2\\\} \Rightarrow P(X \le 2) = \frac{7}{8}$ :x: $F(2) = \frac{7}{8}$


Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Use the example in the second example, compute the probability, PMF, and PDF of the following if applicable.
  1. $X = 1$
  2. $X < 3$
  3. $X \le -1$
  4. $X \le 3$
  5. $X \le 4$
Exercise 2: What is the sum of all PMFs $\sum P(X = x)$ in exercise 1 and for an abitrary random experiment?
Exercise 3: Throw a die twice. X is the sum of numbers rolled. What is p(7)? What is F(3)?
Exercise 4: Extract 3 balls from a box containing an equal number of white and black balls. Put the ball back into the box after each extraction. How many white balls can occur and what are the associated probabilities, PMFs, and PDFs?


Continuous RV - Probability

A continuous random variable $X$ is a function $X: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ where $\Omega$ is an uncountabe set. The normal distribution mentioned in Math for AI 104 is one of the most well-known probability models for continuous random variables .

Let’s see a couple of examples.

  1. Imagine we’re looking at the second hand of a clock and take a random snapshot at an unknown moment during a one-minute period.
    • Define $X(0, 12]$ = angle $\theta$ (in degrees) between the second hand and the 12 o’clock position.
    • The second hand sweeps smoothly in a full circle ($360^\circ$) every minute.
    • So $X \in (0, 360]$.
  2. Adult female/male heights.
    • A person’s height can be any positive real number.
    • So $X \in (0, \infty)$.

PMF for continuous random variables is always 0 since the sample space is so large that it makes the occurence of one value become insignificant. On the other hand, PDF for continuous random varibles can be computed using the area under its curve like Gaussian function.

Mathematical Expectations

Below are some concepts used for discrete random variables. We’ll briefly go over mathematical expectations for continous random variables right after.

Expected Value

Expected value of a discrete random variable X, denoted by $E[X]$, represents the weighted average value of X and computed as follows. It is often referred to as the mean of probability distribution. It is tremendously useful when the size of the sample space is unknown.

\[E[X] = \sum_{k} x_k \cdot P(X = x_k) = \sum_{k} x_k \cdot p(x_k)\]

Some important properties of expected values are

  • $E[\alpha X] = \alpha E[X]$
  • $E[\alpha X + b] = \alpha E[X] + b$.

Variance

Variance of a random variable X, denoted as $var(X)$, is the weighted average of squared distance from the mean. The reason behind squared distance is that we want to variance to be non-negative for further statistics concepts. On top of that, squared is preferred over absolute value since such a squared function is differentiable everywhere.

\[var(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = \sum_{k} (x_k - \mu)^2 p(x_k) = E[X^2] - \mu^2 = E[X^2] - E[X]^2\]

where $\mu = E[X]$.

Standard Deviation

Standard deviation of a random variable X, denoted $\sigma(X)$, is the weighted average of distance from the mean.

\[\sigma(X) = \sqrt{var(X)}\]

:pushpin: Note: (discussed more in Math for AI 106)

  1. If outcomes are equally likely to happen and $N$ is the entire population’s size, we have
\[E[X] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k} x_k \text{ and } var(X) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k} (x_k - \mu)^2.\]
  1. If we only take a sample of size $n$, then N becomes $n - 1$.

Continuous Random Variable

Since PMFs for continuous random variables are always 0, we can only apply the idea to compute expected value, variance, and standard deviations rather than exactly the same formulas. Instead we use integral for parts involving expected value which is

\[\mu = E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x) \,dx.\]

This integral can be done using either Riemann, Lebesgue, or other integrals. The former is applied for “nice” distribution while the latter can handle more complicated distributions. This is partly because the Lebesgue integral takes weighted coefficients into account better. Computers use the Lebesgue integral as its default method.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Toss a coin three times in a roll. Let a random variable be the number of heads in each sequence. Compute the expected value.
Exercise 2: Toss a coin twice. Let a random variable be the number of heads in each sequence. Compute the variance.
Exercise 3: Compute the expected value, variance, and standard derivation given X as follows.
  1. $X = \\{1, 3, 4, 4\\}$
  2. $X = \\{1, 2, 8, 5\\}$
  3. $X = \\{1, 3, 4, 4\\}$ and corresponding $p(X) = \\{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 40.3\\}$
  4. $X = \\{0, 1\\}$ and corresponding $p(X) = \\{p, 1 - p\\}$
  5. $X \le 4$
Exercise 4: A person pays $1 for a lottery ticket. They'll gain $50 if winning with the likelihood of $\frac{1}{100}$; otherwise, nothing. If they do this for a while, would they gain and lose money? How much percentage?
Exercise 5: What is variance of shooting a board if the probability of shooting inside is 0.8? The mean is also 0.8.
Exercise 6: What is variance of $-\sqrt{6}, -\sqrt{5}, -\sqrt{4}. -1, 0, 1, \sqrt{4}, \sqrt{5}, \sqrt{6}$?
Exercise 7: What is variance of a constant?
Exercise 8: Prove the properties of expected values.
Exercise 9: Prove the third equality in the variance formula.
Exercise 10: Throw a die. Consider the number on each side is a random variable of this experiment. Compute the expected value, variance, and standard derivation.
Exercise 11: Write programs for exercises when applicable using numpy.

Covariance and Correlation

:question: We’ve been dealing with cases with only one random variable. What if we’d like to know the relationship between two random variables?

This is where covariance and correlation come into play.

Covariance

Covariance measures the linear relationship of two random variables, that is, how they change together. Recall $n - 1$ is for samples as we consider $X$ and $Y$ as subset of the population.

\[cov(X, Y) = E[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)] = \frac{\sum(x - \mu_X)(y - \mu_Y)}{n - 1}\]

where $X$ and $Y$ are random variables such that $E[X] = \mu_X$ and $E[Y] = \mu_Y$.

We deduce from the above formula that $var(X) = cov(X, X)$. Formally, covariance is represented using the following 2 by 2 matrix

\[\begin{bmatrix} var(X) & cov(X, Y) \\ cov(X, Y) & var(Y) \end{bmatrix}.\]

We can interpret the result as follows.

  • $cov(X, Y) \in (-\infty, \infty)$.
  • $cov(X, Y) = cov(Y, X)$.
  • If it is positive covariance or $cov(X, Y) > 0$, then $X$ increases implies $Y$’s rise on average.
  • If it is negative covariance or $cov(X, Y) < 0$, then $X$ reduces implies $Y$’s decrease on average.
  • If it is zero covariance or $cov(X, Y) = 0$, then there is no linear correlation between two random variables.

Correlation

Even though covariance is useful, its value can be unnecessarily large. In addition, covariance only indicates the direction of the relationship, not how much it is. To address these issues, we standardize the covariance to obtain the correlation coefficient.

Correlation is a statistical measure the quantifies the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two random variables. It is also often represented as a 2 by 2 matrix like covariance.

\[\begin{align*} corr(X, Y) & = \frac{cov(X, Y)}{\sigma_X \cdot \sigma_Y} = \frac{cov(X, Y)}{\sqrt{var(X)} \cdot \sqrt{var(Y)}} \\ & = \frac{n (\sum_{i} x_i y_i) - (\sum_i x_i) (\sum_i y_i)}{\sqrt{n (\sum_{i} x_i^2) - (\sum_{i} x_i)^2} \cdot \sqrt{n (\sum_{i} y_i^2) - (\sum_{i} y_i)^2}} \end{align*}\]

We can interpret the result as follows.

  • $corr(X, Y) \in [-1, 1]$.
  • $corr(X, Y) = corr(Y, X)$.
  • If it is positive correlation or $corr(X, Y) > 0$, then $X$ increases implies $Y$’s rise on average.
    • If $corr(X, Y) = 1$, values of $X$ and $Y$ form a straight line with a positive slope.
    • If $corr(X, Y)$ is close to 1, then it is a strong relationship and values of $X$ and $Y$ lie close to a straight line.
    • If $corr(X, Y)$ is not so close to 1, then it is a weaker relationship and values of $X$ and $Y$ are distributed around but further away from a straight line.
  • If it is negative covariance or $corr(X, Y) < 0$, then $X$ reduces implies $Y$’s decrease on average.
    • If $corr(X, Y) = -1$, values of $X$ and $Y$ form a straight line with a negative slope.
    • If $corr(X, Y)$ is close to -1, then it is a strong relationship and values of $X$ and $Y$ lie close to a straight line.
    • If $corr(X, Y)$ is not so close to -1, then it is a weaker relationship and values of $X$ and $Y$ are distributed around but further away from a straight line.
  • If it is zero covariance or $corr(X, Y) = 0$, then there is no linear relationship between two random variables and values scatter without a clear linear pattern.

Continuous Random Variable

Like mathematical expectations, we cannot directly compute covariance and correlation of continuous random variables. In this case, we can convert continous random variables to discrete ones using Monte Carlo method. Softwares may have it set up in methods as follows.

# X ~ N(0, 1) 
# Y ~ (0.5, 1.5)
data1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, 1000)
data2 = np.random.normal(0.5, 1.5, 1000)

# calculate covariance and correlation matrix
covariance_matrix = np.cov(data1, data2)
correlation_matrix = np.corrcoef(data1, data2)
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Compute their covariance and correlation for X and Y below. Determine their relationship in detail.
  1. $X = \\{1, 3, 4, 4\\}$ and $Y = \\{1, 2, 3, 2\\}$
  2. $X = \\{1, 1, 2, 4\\}$ and $Y = \\{2, 3, 4, 3\\}$
Exercise 2: Prove the third equality of correlation formula.
Exercise 3: Prove that $corr(X, Y) \in [-1, 1]$.
Exercise 4: Prove that $corr(X, Y) = \pm 1$ implies values of X and Y are on a straight line.
Exercise 5: Write programs for exercises when applicable using numpy.


:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
Are there any cases where continuous random variables are converted to discrete random variables for easier computations? Yes. We can use Monte Carlo method to make it happen. We divide uncountable values into bins/classes/intervals which are considered single values, then use naive Bayes or histogram. For example, salaries can be categorized into groups like low, medium, and high.
Resources for Applied Statistics Storytelling with Data: A Data Visualization Guide for Business Professionals by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Statistics: The Art and Science of Learning from Data by Alan Agresti, Introduction to Probability by Blitzstein
How do Riemman and Lebesgue integrals work? Riemman integral is like accounting, accummulating bit by bit. Lebesgue integral is like a cashier taking money, putting money into their own category and summing them up in the end.
Why n - 1 for sample? This is called Bessel’s correction in Statistics. When using sample, selected value points tend to lie closer to the sample mean than the population mean. Thus, using n makes values’ distribution (variance/standard deviation) is lower than what it really is. Taking n - 1 is a way to make up for it to address bias, helping the result reflect the distribution of the population better. When writing code, use ddof = 1 for variance and standard deviation computations.
How are these expectations used in Machine Learning? They can be used in optimization problems. In some cases, models need to take actions that maximize expectations in game theory. Basically, “learning” in Machine Learning is to find models so that average expectation errors are the least insignificant.

Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Vinh-Dinh Nguyen’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read Math for AI 104 or been familiar with probability and statistics. Note that only basic probability material is introduced here; we’ll pick up specific concepts when in need.

________quote____________________
-quoter’s name

In today’s post, we’ll explore some descriptive statistics and probability distribution theory. We’ll also discuss some applications in AI including image processing.

Descriptive Statistics refers to tools that summarize and describe features of a dataset, providing us with a clearer picture of the data. There are three main categories: central tendency, variability, and distribution.

Measure of Central Tendency

Mean and Expected Value

Expected value is not considered a measure of central tendency, but this concept and mean are closely related as they both represent some sort of average.

Mean Expected Value
Given a dataset of N items $X = \\{X_1, \cdots, X_N\\}$
$$\mu_{X} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i$$ where $X_i$ is a specific outcome. $$E(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i P(X = X_i)$$ where $X_i$ is a specific outcome and $P(X = X_i)$ is the probability of a specific outcome.
  • the average of all values in the dataset
  • we've already collected all raw data
  • Example: Consider playing a guessing game 100 times (in the detailed example below). We can only compute the mean once we've already played 100 times.
  • the weighted average of all values in the dataset
  • this value is what we expect to occur before collecting data
  • Example: Consider playing a guessing game 100 times (in the detailed example below). We have either played it just a few times or never played it before but have some statistics on it. We can use such given data to predict what we may end up.


Example: Are you willing to play this game?
Problem statement: We have information of 100 students in AIO2025: 30 of them love Math while the remaining does not. Let's play a game 100 times where you must guess whether the next student who joins the course loves Math or does not. The rule is
  • If the student loves Math, you'll lose \$1.
  • If the student doesn't love Math, you'll gain \$1.
Breakdown: To make a smart decision, we should know
  • The money you'll lose/gain if you randomly select a student in AIO2025 and it turns out they love Math.
  • The money you'll lose/gain if you randomly select a student in AIO2025 and it turns out they do not love Math.
Idea: With this information, we can analyze the likelihood of outcomes for the two student groups and evaluate whether this game works in your favor.
  1. Compute the money gain/loss after playing 100 times for each case and the whole data.
    Love Math Not Love Math Total
    Number of students 30 70 100
    Probability $30\% = 0.3$ $70\% = 0.7$ $100\% = 1.0$
    Outcome $-7$1$ $+\$1$
    Expected number gains/losses $100 \cdot 0.3 = 30$ $100 \cdot 0.7 = 70$
    Expected gain (a negative number is a loss) $30 \cdot -1 = -30$ $70 \cdot +1 = +70$ $-30 + 70 = \$40$
    After playing this game 100 times in a roll, you would expect to gain \$40 in total.
  2. The average amount of money you expect to gain per game is $40 / 100 = \$0.4$.
  3. Using the method above we compute the expectation as follows. $$E[X] = \frac{[(0.3 \cdot 100) \cdot (-1)] + [(0.7 \cdot 100) \cdot (+1)]}{100} = 0.4$$
  4. If using the expected value formula, we have a very similar calculation $$E[X] = \sum x \cdot P(X = x) = (-1 \cdot 0.3) + (+1 \cdot 0.7) = 0.4$$
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Given $X = \\{2, 8, 5, 4, 1, 4\\}$, compute the mean of this dataset.
Exercise 2: We'll play a similar guessing game as in the example. The rule is that you'll gain $10 if the student loves Math, otherwise you'll lose $1. Are you willing to play this time?


Median

Given a dataset of N items $X = \{X_1, \cdots, X_N\}$, median is the value dividing the sorted dataset in half. To obtain the median, we follow two steps.

  1. Sort $X$.
  2. Calculate the median $m$:
    • If $N$ is odd, then $m = X_{\frac{N + 1}{2}}$.
    • If $N$ is even, then $m = \frac{1}{2} (X_{\frac{N}{2}} + X_{\frac{N + 1}{2}})$.

-Dr. Thai-Ha Nguyen

In today’s post, we’ll explore Git and GitHub. They are essential tools any developer or engineer should be familiar with. We can use them for personal and collaborative purposes.

Let’s implant some analogies of Git and GitHub in mind before delving into both. Git is like a camera capturing snapshots of a project continuously. GitHub is like Google Photos storing all photos from Git to cloud so that we can review and share with anyone at any point in time.

Git Principles and Configuration

Version Control System (VCS)

VCS is a general term for Git. VCS is a system that tracks and saves changes of files over time. It contains all information about

  • what has been changed
  • who has changed it
  • when it was changed
  • why it was changed.

With these properties, this system enables us to

  • revert to previous working state when bugs/errors/mistakes have been made
  • compare the difference between two versions
  • show related change information
  • protect data and support collaboration.

There are three types of VCS:

  1. Local VCS is the very first VCS for one-person use. That is, everything is saved locally in a computer, so there is no way to recover if the computer quits working and it’s difficult to share your work with others.

  2. Centralized VCS (CVCS), for example Subversion and CVS, is another old VCS where developers use one single server to store their work. Even though it facilitates seamless collaboration, it totally depends on the centralized server. This would be catastrophic if the server corrupted. Users wouldn’t be able to save versioned changes or collaborate with others.

  3. Distributed VCS (DVCS), for example Git and Mercurial, is the currently-used VCS where each developer has their own server. That is, every user has a local copy of complete projects and history at all times. If their server is inaccessible, they can always create a new one and share their work with others. Thus, it is complete, secure, and flexible.

Git

Git is a DVCS created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, who is the father of Linux. He designed Git to manage Linux source code since Linux is developed by thousands of people from all over the place. Git is widely adopted just a short while after its creation as it is simple, lightweight, instantaneous, and easy to branch and distribute.

SSO Principles

  1. Snapshot instead of diff
    • Git snaps an entire project after each change (when committing) to capture all changes at once.
    • If there’s no change, Git creates a link to the old version to save storage capacity.
  2. SHA-1 Data Integrity
    • Git protects data by the SHA-1 function with unique identifiers—40-character hash codes like ID (for each commit).
    • when content alters, so does its hash code, which ensures commit integrity.
  3. Offline-first
    • Git allows us to work and save your progress offline (commit).
    • We only need the Internet when pull/push.

Configuration
After installation, some basic configurations can be done for Git are

  • git config –global user.name your_name:
  • git config –global user.email your_email
  • git config –global core.editor “code-wait”
  • git config –global color.ui auto

They are all automatically imported into a file on our computer. We can use git config –list to see them.

An alias for a command statement is very useful while we work with Git. It is to replace a long word/phrase with a short user-defined name.

git log shows history of your work which may be prolix. We can customize the output so that it is clear, concise, and pretty.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read SQL for AI 102, had some coding experience, and known a bit of AI knowledge. Absolute beginners are encouraged to read the material and repeatedly practice coding without AI assistance to strengthen their coding and code-reading skills. Note that only necessary Python knowledge is introduced here.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who could have known nothing about database or have had some experience working with data. Absolute beginners are encouraged to read and practice the basics without AI assistance to familiarize themselves with the material. Note that only necessary SQL knowledge is introduced here.

________quote____________________
-quoter’s name

In today’s post, we’ll explore SQL in Data Analysis, specifically subqueries, procedure and trigger, and some advanced topics.

SQL Join

In practice, we regularly want to obtain information from at least two tables. SQL join refers to various methods of combining tables together to retrieve meanningful information. Data extraction is a key part of data mining that helps us better understand databases. Furthermore, we can apply Machine Learning algorithms to uncover patterns, gain insights, and make predictions based on broader trends in the data.

INNER JOIN

INNER JOIN or JOIN is to read data that several tables have in common. This is similar to taking intersection of sets in Python. We can think of considering one table and taking only parts that contain the other tables.

WHERE statement can also perform this action, but JOIN is preferred for this purpose, especially in large databases.

  • INNER JOIN is an explicit join syntax which separates join logic from filtering logic
  • WHERE is an implicit join syntax which does not.

Two Tables 

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
INNER JOIN table_name_2 tb2 
    ON tb1.common_column_name = tb2.common_column_name;

This query says, take only rows whose data on common column from table 1 match with that from table 2. Swapping tables’ names provides the same result by definition.

DEMONSTRATION and EXPLANATION

Three or More Tables
We can use more INNER JOIN or JOIN statements to obtain the intersection of multiple tables.

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
INNER JOIN table_name_2 tb2
    ON tb1.common_column_name_12 = tb2.common_column_name_12
INNER JOIN table_name_3 tb3
    ON tb1.common_column_name_13 = tb2.common_column_name_13
...
INNER JOIN table_name_n tbn
    ON tbk.common_column_name_kn = tbn.common_column_name_kn;

DEMONSTRATION

SELF JOIN

SELECT *
FROM table_name tb1
JOIN table_name tb2
    ON tb1.column_name_1 = tb2.column_name_2;

SELF JOIN is the inner join of a table with itself. We can use this concept when values of two separate columns in a table belong to the same group.

DEMONSTRATION and EXPLANATION

Compound Join Condition

Recall that a table can have a composite key. If we want to join it with another table using these columns, we can modify the regular inner join as follows.

SELECT *
FROM table_name_1 tb1
INNER JOIN table_name_2 tb2
    ON tb1.column_name_1 = tb2.column_name_1
    AND tb1.column_name_2 = tb2.column_name_2
    ...
    AND tb1.column_name_n = tb2.column_name_n;

OUTER JOIN

If we have two tables, OUTER JOIN retrieves data from at least one of them including matched information. There are three types: LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, and FULL JOIN. While the last one takes both tables, the rest only takes only one, either left or right table.

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
LEFT JOIN table_name_2 tb2 
    ON tb1.common_column_name = tb2.common_column_name;

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
RIGHT JOIN table_name_2 tb2 
    ON tb1.common_column_name = tb2.common_column_name;

USING Clause

If common columns from tables have the same name, it’s unnecessary to rewrite it many times. Instead, we can simplify the query. This is extremely useful for compound join conditions.

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
JOIN table_name_2 tb2 
    USING (common_column_name);

UNION

UNION is to retrieve all conditional data from several tables. This is similar to taking union of sets in Python.

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
WHERE condition_1
UNION
SELECT * FROM table_name_2 tb2
WHERE condition_2
UNION
...
UNION
SELECT * FROM table_name_n tbn
WHERE condition_n;

SQL Temporary Queries

In numerical data analysis, it’s often useful to aggregate values by group, with summation and average being one of the most commonly used operations. We can solve this problem either directly or indirectly.

GROUP BY - SUM

We use necessary statements to manipulate data as usual.

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
JOIN table_name_2 tb2 
    USING (common_column_name)
GROUP BY tb2.column_name_group
SUM(tb2.column_name_sum);

There are two mandatory operations in this query template. GROUP BY allows us to group data with the same name together. Then, SUM automatically sums up values for each group. For average, use AVG.

Common Table Expression (CTE) WITH … AS

We can create a temporary table where data are managed and call it afterwards. Just like a function, the data in this table is only created on call.

WITH temp_table_name AS (
    SELECT column_names, SUM(column_name_sum) AS temp_column_name
    FROM table_name_2 tb2
    GROUP BY column_name_group
    SUM(column_name_sum)
)

SELECT * FROM table_name_1 tb1
JOIN temp_table_name
USING (common_column_name);

WITH clause acts as a function with temp_table_name as the function name. We can reuse this temporary table whenever it is needed. Since there is only one table in the clause, there is no point specifying where those columns come from.

EXAMPLE, DEMONSTRATION, and EXPLANATION

Subqueries

In cases where we want to avoid JOIN and GROUP BY, we can apply subqueries.

SELECT column_names,
       (SELECT SUM(column_name_sum)
       FROM table_name_2 tb2
       WHERE tb1.common_column_name = common_column_name) AS temp_column_name
FROM table_name_1 tb1;

The query inside parentheses is called a subquery. It is calculated first based on the condition given in the main query.

Temporary Table

Even though CTE and subqueries are convenient, reevaluation is executed every time they are called.

:question: You may concern, How can we save the outcome of such a query so that it saves resources and is still reusable?

Instead of a shallow temporary table as above, we can create a deep temporary table and insert required operations. This momentary table “lives” throughout a session but disappears entirely when the session ends.

CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE temp_table_name (
    column_names DATATYPE
);

INSERT INTO temp_table_name 
SELECT column_names, 
       SUM(column_name_sum) AS temp_column_name
FROM table_name_2 tb2
GROUP BY column_name_group;

SQL Stored Procedure and Trigger

As mentioned, temporary tables are like renters—staying for a limited time while they’re officially signed with their landlord (the database session). Though they can be very useful for storing intermediate results or simplifying complex queries, they have limitations, such as limited lifespan and lack of persistence after the session ends. As such, we want to store the temporary table in a place where we can grab and use it any time.

Stored Procedure

A stored procedure is essentially a precompiled function of SQL statements stored within a database, designed for efficient and reusable execution of database operations. Once it is created, we can CALL it.

DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE procedure_name()
BEGIN
    -- SQL statements
END;
//
DELIMITER;

CALL procedure_name();

Using the previous section’s example, we can place the temporary table where SQL statements go. It will then be executed whenever our session starts.

DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE procedure_name()
BEGIN
    DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp_table_name;
    CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE temp_table_name (
        column_names DATATYPE
    );

    INSERT INTO temp_table_name 
    SELECT column_names, 
        SUM(column_name_sum) AS temp_column_name
    FROM table_name_2 tb2
    GROUP BY column_name_group; 
END;
//
DELIMITER;

Trigger

One advantage when working with any computer program or software is that actions can possibly be logged somewhere. SQL is not an exception.

A trigger is a set of SQL statements that run and log every time specific oprations are conducted such as inserting, updating, or deleting a row.

CREATE TRIGGER trigger_name
AFTER [INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE]  ON table_name
FOR EACH ROW
-- SQL statements

AFTER can be replaced with BEFORE depending on users’ requirement. We can choose one of the three available operations.

entry.title: Math for AI 104
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read Math for AI 103 or been familiar with probability and statistics. Note that only basic Probability material is introduced here; we’ll pick up specific concepts when in need.

Our world operates based on creativity, so we should always be ready to be creative. If we are given a task and it cannot be completed using available tools. It is a good signal that we can be creative to make great things happen.
-Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh

In today’s post, we’ll explore Naive Bayes Classifier and Gaussian Function. We’ll also discuss some applications in AI including classification problems.

Classification Problem Overview

A classification problem in machine learning involves training a model to learn patterns and predict outcomes based on specific input data. Outcomes or targets, often listed in a classifying column, is called a class, category, label, or ground truth. Ground truth is commonly used for image datasets. Input data, listed in other columns, is named a feature.

In the table above, there are three features including “Confident”, “Studied”, and “Sick”. Using them, we want to a model to provide some value of the class “Result”.

Review

Recall $A$ and $B$ are independent events if the occurence of A remains unaffected by that of B and vice versa, that is, $P(AB) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \text{ or } P(A | B) = P(A) \text{ or } P(B | A) = P(B)$. This concept significantly simplifies the process of working with large datasets since we only need to know the probability of events separately.

Events $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ if and only if

\[P(AB | C) = P(A | C) \cdot P(B | C) \text{ where } P(C) > 0.\]

Recall for a complete system $A_1, \cdots, A_n$ and an event $H$, Total Probability Theorem says

\[P(H) = P(H_1) + \cdots + P(H_n) = P(A_1) \cdot P(H | A_1) + \cdots + P(A_n) \cdot P(H | A_n).\]

The likelihood of Ai and that of H given Ai is true are included since the occurence of event H only makes sense when event Ai has happened. In classification problems, features only become meaningful to a training dataset within the context of the class. Without classes, models have no reference point to interpret what the features represent.

Bayes’ Rule says if $X$ is an event and $c$ is an element of a complete system ${C_1, \cdots, C_n}$ with $P(C_i) \neq 0$, then

\[P(C_i | X) = \frac{P(C_i) \cdot P(X | C_i)}{P(X)} = \frac{P(C_i) \cdot P(X | C_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(C_j) \cdot P(X | C_j)}.\]

:pushpin: Note: The fact that such unrealistic assumptions are made gives right to the word naive in the Naive Bayes algorithm, which derives $P(AB) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$. For example, when we use this formula to classify emails with the word “Free Money”, it says P(Free Money) = P(Money Free) or “Free” is unrelated to “Money”, which is often not true. See practice exercises for detailed computations.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Using the following table, analyze the relationship between "Studied" and "Result" in each situation?
  1. P(Studied = No, Result = Fail)
  2. P(Studied = Yes, Result = Fail)
  3. P(Studied = No, Result = Pass)
  4. P(Studied = Yes, Result = Pass)
Exercise 2: Using the above table assume that the relationships between "Studied" and "Result" and "Sick" and "Result" are both independent, analyze the probability of "Studied" and "Sick" given "Result" in each situation?
  1. P(Studied = No, Sick = Yes | Result = Pass)
  2. P(Studied = Yes, Sick = No | Result = Fail)
  3. P(Studied = Yes, Sick = Yes | Result = Fail)
Exercise 3: Out of 6 students, there are 3 passes and 3 fails. Out of passes, there is one student who didn't study. Out of fails, there are two. What is the probability of a student who didn't study?
Exercise 4: Can two dependent events be conditionally independent? Explain why or why not. Provide an example.
Exercise 5: Can two independent events be conditionally dependent? Explain why or why not. Provide a proof if possible. Provide an example.


Bernoulli Naive Bayes Classifier (BNBC) for Discrete Random Variable (RV)

Bernoulli Naive Bayes is a machine learning algorithm tailored for discrete and binary-valued feature problems. Binary-valued features can be Yes/No or True/False. It uses conditional probabilities to make predictions, whether we’re working with one feature or many at once.

One feature

We talked about this in the previous post. Try out practice exercises to familiarize yourself with it.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Use feature "Studied" and "Result" of the empirical table. Compute the probability that a student studied/didn't student given their result. Exercise 2: Solve exercise 1 without the formula.
Hints: What is $\sum_{i} P(Studied | Pass)$?


Multiple Features

For multiple-featured problems, apply Bayes’ Rule and conditional independence assumptions.

Let $C$ be a class and $X_1, \cdots, X_n$ be features (also known as random variables introduced in Math for AI 105 Warm-up). The formula for the probability of an event given a few other events has already occurred.

\[P(C | X_1, \cdots, X_n) = \frac{P(X_1, \cdots, X_n | C)P(C)}{P(X_1, \cdots, X_n)} = \frac{P(X_1 | C) \cdots P(X_n | C) \cdot P(C)}{\sum_{k} P(X_1, \cdots, X_n | C_k)}\]

where $C_k$’s are all labels.

Practice Exercises
The naive assumptions are applied in both exercises.
Exercise 1: Let R, Co, St, and Si be random variables short for "Result", "Confident", "Studied", and "Sick". Compute $P(R | Co, St, Si)$ where R = Pass, Co = Yes, St = Yes, Si = Yes. Exercise 2: Ignore the last row, what is the relationship among random variables given the target column is "Confident"?

Gaussian Function

:question: All we’ve been through so far involves events where we can count the number of features. You may wonder, what if given datasets contain continuous values which lie within a given range instead of a finite set?

Definition

A distribution is a collection of data shared among a range of values on a variable.

The probability distribution for a random variable describes how the occurence of possible outcomes for an experiment are distributed over that variable. Its graph is bell-shaped, maybe skewed or not, as in figure. The Gaussian function is its special type known as normal distribution where its graph is symmetric bell-shaped curve as in figures.

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]

where

  • $-\infty < x < \infty$
  • $\mu_{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ is mean of the dataset $X$
  • $\sigma^2 = var(X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \mu)^2$ is the variance of the dataset $X$.

DEMONSTRATION

It’s worth pointing out a few fascinating properties of Gaussian distribution graph.

  • The graphs are symmetric bell-shaped curve.
  • Changing $\mu$ or $\sigma^2$ doesn’t change the bell shape of the normal distribution—it either shifts or stretches the standard graph (Figure ).
  • Any Gaussuan distribution can be converted to a standard normal distribution.
  • The area under the curve of the standard graph is $1$.

The third characteristic implies that we can use its area function as probability for continuous random variables with area being always non-negative and uninterrupted. For example, for the Iris flower case, the length and width can be any real number within some range. Thus using a function that can handle continuity like Gaussian would solve the problem.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Using figure , describe how the shape of standard Gaussian function graph is shifted or stretched as $\mu$ or $\sigma^2$ does?
Exercise 2: Show that the area under the curve of the standard normal distribution is 1 using integral from $-\infty$ to $\infty$.
Exercise 3: Write a program that computes Gaussian function given $\mu = 0, \sigma^2 = 1, \text{ and } x = [-4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3]$.
Exercise 4: Given the following information, determine which Gaussian function has greater area under the curve?
  • $\mu = 1.52, \sigma^2 = 0.1416$
  • $\mu = 3.88, \sigma^2 = 0.0776$


:bulb: Applications in AI
A Gaussian filter uses the Gaussian function to obtain a weighted avergae of surrounding pixels in Image Smoothing. A bilateral filter uses this concept with information of pixel color to perform better on edges of objects.

Central Limit Theorem is the idea of using a sample—a subset of the entire population—for analysis. You can take any example, but here we’ll use an image whose population contains pixel colors of the entire image. First, randomly select 30 pixels and compute their color mean. We repeat this process 10000 times. Eventually we can create a histogram of these averages. Even if the original values of the entire population are not normally distributed, the sample’s mean values are inclined to be.

Gaussian Naive Bayes Classifier (GNBC) for Continuous RV

Gaussian Naive Bayes is a machine learning algorithm that combines the Gaussian function and Bayes’ Theorem to solve continuous feature problems.

One Feature

The probability at one value $P(X | C) = 0$ at all times in the case of continuous random variables. So, if we use a real probability function, it’s impossible to make sense of a dataset. Instead, we want a different function that can capture the idea of likelihood. That function is called probability density function, which measures the density around a value. The higher the density is, the more likely the value is relative to others. As Gaussian area function acts as probability, the Gaussian function itself becomes such a density function.

\[P(X | C) = f(X | C) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp^{-\frac{(X-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]

where $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are the mean and variance class $C$.

:pushpin: Note: The density function can be evaluated greater than 1 when the graph narrows down and stretches. This is valid because the total area is still 1, which satisfies the probability concept all the probabilities are from 0 to 1.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Given the following, compute $P(Length = 3.0)$.
  • $P(Cat = 0) = 0.5$
  • $P(Cat = 1) = 0.5$
  • $f(Length = 3.0 | Cat = 0) = 0.01$
  • $f(Length = 3.0 | Cat = 1) = 0.01$

Exercise 2: Use the following table to compute the probability of each category given the length is 3.0 units. Exercise 3: What is the sum of the probabilities in exercise 2. Explain why it is that value.
Exercise 4: Write a program to compute the probability in exercise 2.
Hints: Use two ways: using algorithm and using packages
Exercise 5: Can "Length" be the category? Explain why or why not.


Multiple Features

As we’ve seen the Iris flower table has two features. This means we can use the probability of each category given both of them.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: How many Gaussian functions do we need to compute the probability of each category given two features? Exercise 2: Use the above table to compute the probability of each category given the length is 4.1 units and the width is 2.9 units.
Exercise 3: Write a program to compute the probability in exercise 2.
Hints: Use two ways: using algorithm and using packages.
Exercise 4: What is the sum of the probabilities in exercise 2? Explain why it is that value.
Exercise 5: Use the following table and compute the probability of each category given both features.


Multiple Features - Multiple Classes

We can definitely apply the same idea to compute the probability where there are multiple features and multiple classes.

Practice Exercises
Use the following table to compute the probability of each category given the length is 5.2 units and the width is 2.4 units.

:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
Is dependence or independence better for AI? It doesn’t matter. AI can handle both.
Based on data, can I test if two features are dependent? Yes. You can use Chi-Square test of independence.
Why does nature generally have Gaussian distribution? Many variables in nature arise as the sum of many small and independent factors. According to the Central Limit Theorem, such variables tend to approximate a Gaussian distribution.
Diistinguish probability distribution and probability density functions. A probability distribution function applies to all random variables while a probability density function applies to continuous only.

entry.title: Math for AI 103
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have known arithmetics or been familiar with probability and statistics. Note that only basic probability material is introduced in this Math for AI series; we’ll pick up specific concepts when in need. To complete some practice exercises, learners should know basic coding or read Python for AI 106.

In today’s post, we’ll explore basic probability including Total Probability Theorem and Bayes’ Rule. We’ll go over some AI-related practice problems and an application called simple binary classification.

Basic Concepts

Probability is a way to mathematicalize our real-life incidents. We’ll first look at terminolgy used to talk about those incidents formally.

Defintions

An experiment is a planned operation through which specific results are obtained. Some examples are , flipping a coin, and rolling a die.

An outcome is a result of an experiment. If we put all possible outcomes together in a set, we call it the sample space denoted by $\Omega$ in this post.

  • Possible outcomes are displayed within braces $\{\}$.
  • We can represent it in three following ways, which are demonstrated in later examples in this post,
    • list all possible outcomes
    • create a Venn diagram
    • create a tree diagram.

An event is a part/subset of the sample space, usually mentioned using capital letters. It can be any combination of outcomes. There are three main types based on how likely an event is to happen.

  • Certain event: an event that always occurs in an experiment, denoted by $\Omega$.
  • Impossible event: an event that never occurs in an experiment, denoted by $\emptyset$.
  • Random event: an even that may or may not occur in an experiment. An experiment whose outcomes are random events is called a random experiment.

We mostly work with random events and how to learn and hanlde their randomness. It’s like the law exists to guide and regulate people’s behavior, helping maintain order and fairness in society. Or analyzing stock prices is to identify the patterns, predict their future trends, and making informed investment decisions.

Let’s take a look at some examples. Assume that the coin, die, and card deck are fair and regular.

Experiment Outcome Sample Space Event Probability
Flipping a coin {head} {head, tail} {tail} $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = 50\%$
Rolling a die {5} {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} {Die is odd} = {1, 3, 5} $\frac{3}{6} = 0.5 = 50\%$
Picking a card out of a deck {ace of heart} a set of 52 cards {Card is a club} = a set of 13 clubs $\frac{13}{52} = 0.25 = 25\%$


Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: A family has 2 children. Which of the following is a certain, random, or impossible event?
  • A = "A family has 1 boy and 1 girl."
  • B = "A family has 3 children."
  • C = "A family has 2 children."
Exercise 2: A box contains 8 balls: 6 blue and 2 read. Pick randomly 3 balls. Which of the following is a certain, random, or impossible event?
  • A = "we get 3 blue balls."
  • B = "we get 3 red balls."
  • C = "we get 3 balls."
Exercise 3:


Operations on Events

Consider two events A and B from the same experiment. Since events are sets, we certainly can perform set operations on them as follows. They are demonstrated by colored regions in the figures below. A is the cirle on the left and B is the circle on the right.

Notation Operation Name Description
$A \cap B$ or $AB$ Intersection Both A and B happen
$A \cup B$ or $A + B$ Union Either A or B or both happen
$A^\complement$ or $A^\prime$ or $\overline{A}$ Complement A does not happen


The following example is solved by listing all possible outcomes in each event.

  Description Mathematical Result
Sample Space Rolling a die {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
Event A Rolling an even number {2, 4, 6}
Event B Rolling a number divisible by 3 {3, 6}
$AB$ Rolling a number that is even and divisible by 3 {6}
$A + B$ Rolling a number that is either even or divisible by 3 {2, 3, 4, 6}
$A^\prime$ Rolling a number that is not even {1, 3, 5}


Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Roll a die. Use Venn digrams to illustrate events $A, B, C, AC, AD, A + D, A^\prime, B^\prime, AF, \text{ and } F + G $.
  • A = "The number rolled is odd."
  • B = "The number rolled is even."
  • C = "The number rolled is less than 3."
  • D = "The number rolled is greater than 3."
  • E = "The number rolled is greater than 4."
  • F = "The number rolled is greater than or equal to 3."
  • G = "The number rolled is less than 2."
Exercise 2: Write operation to describe the following diagrams. A is the cirle on the left and B is the circle on the right.


Types of Events

When dealing with probability, we often encounter two common types of events which are distinguished concepts. We’ll go over them all using events A and B above in a moment.

Mutually Exclusive Events

$A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events if they cannot both occur simulatenously, that is, they have no elements in common or $A \cap B = \emptyset$. Otherwise, they are non-mutally exclusive.

An example is events A and B from the practice exercise 1 above. Another example is training dataset and testing dataset in a neural network.

Independent Events

$A$ and $B$ are independent events if the occurence of A remains unaffected by that of B and vice versa, that is,

\[P(AB) = P(A) \cdot P(B).\]

$P$ represents the probability of an event which will be discussed in detail in the next section. The concept of dependent/independent events is commonly used to create a tree diagram for implication. This can help answer questions like if a treatment alleviates a disease or if there is a storm in the future with the current kind of weather. The formula derives from multiplication rule mentioned in the next section,

\[P(AB) = P(A) \cdot P(B | A).\]

Here, $P(B | A) = P(B)$ since event A happening does nothing to the occurence of event B.

If A and B are not independent, then they are dependent events.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Roll a die. Let $A = \{ 4 \}$ and $B = \{ 2, 4, 6 \}$. Are A and B independent? Show the calculation.
Exercise 2: Roll a die. Based on the images below, are A and B independent? Show the calculation.

Probability

As mentioned, probability is a way to mathematicalize concepts, managing events’ randomness numerically. Using probability, we can talk about how likely an event occurs rather than making sets of elements.

Probability is the likehood of an event happening. That is, when we conduct a large enough number of experiments, we observe the likelihood converges to some number—it is a probability.

  • $0 \leq P(A) \leq 1$ where A is an event.
  • $P(\Omega) = 1$: if P(A) is close to 1, then it’s very likely that A occurs.
  • $P(\emptyset) = 0$: if P(A) is close to 0, then it’s very unlikely for A to occur.

We approach different types of data in different ways in terms of probability computation. There are three primary methods to describe probability formula: classical probability and geometric probability.

Classical Probability uses sets to perform a computation. We can use this method when sets are finite. Its formula is

\[P(A) = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}} = \frac{n(A)}{n(\Omega)}.\]

We’ll use the same event A from the above example and have

  • $\Omega = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \} \Rightarrow n_{\Omega} = 6$
  • $A = \{ 2, 4, 6 \} \Rightarrow n_{A} = 3$
  • $P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(\Omega)} = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 = 50\%$.

Geometric Probability

For situations where sets are infinite, that is, we cannot count the number of elements, we’ll use geometric probability to carry out calculations instead. It is applied in Genetic Algorithm Optimization or Large Language Models (LLMs) in Machine Learning.

\[P(A) = \frac{\text{measure of domain A}}{\text{measure of domain } \Omega}\]

where domain is the region an event can be.

While length measures the region in 1D, area measures the region in 2D. We’ll go over an example in one dimension.

Let $x$ an arbitrary real number between 0 and 1 inclusively. What is the probability of $x$ between 0 and 0.25?

  • $A = (0, 0.5) \Rightarrow \text{measure of domain A} = \text{length of segment } (0, 0.25) = 0.25$
  • $\Omega = (0, 1) \Rightarrow \text{measure of domain } \Omega = \text{length of segment } (0, 1) = 1$
  • $P(A) = \frac{\text{measure of domain A}}{\text{measure of domain } \Omega} = \frac{0.25}{1} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Example: PI Estimation
Problem statement: Estimate PI using geometry.
Breakdown:
  • $N_s$ is the number of random samples within the square generated according to uniform distribution.
  • $N_c$ is the number of random samples within the circle generated according to uniform distribution.
  • $s = 2 \text{ and } A_s$ are the square side and area, respectively.
  • $r = 1 \text{ and } A_c$ are the circle radius and area, respectively.
Idea: Identify the relation between the number of random samples on each region and the area of such a region and utilize it to obtain their suitable ratios.
  1. The circle is within the square.
    • The square sides are from -1 to 1.
    • The circle is centered at 0 with radius 1.
  2. Identify the relation between the number of random samples on a region and its area.
    • The more the number of random samples is, the more the square/circle is covered.
    • The ratio of area is approximately that of the sample numbers: $\frac{N_c}{N_s} = \frac{A_c}{A_s} = \frac{s^2}{\pi r^2}$
  3. Set the number of random samples on the square. Count the sample number on the circle.
    • Check if a sample is in the circle by using the circle formula.
  4. Use the formula in step 1 to estimate PI.


Emperical/Expiremental Probability is the ratio of the number of event occurences to the number of attempts made. This probability method is solely based on actual data, so it’s imperative the data be accurate and not null and we carefully preprocess it. Note the difference between this probability and the other two is that the sample space varies depending on how many times an experiment is conducted.

\[P(A) = \frac{\text{# of times occured}}{\text{# of times experiment performed}}\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Roll a die. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 3?
Exercise 2: Drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck. What is the probability of getting a king? What is the probability of getting a black card?
Exercise 3: A dart is thrown at a square dartboard such that it will land randomly on the area of the dartboard. What is the probability of it landing on the colored region?
Exercise 4: Write a program that simulates coin flips and estimates the probability of getting a head (or tail).
Exercise 5: Write a program that implements the PI estimation example.


Rules of Probability

Addition Rule refers to the probability of at least one event happening. It is known as inclusion-exclusion principle.

  • Generally, we have

    \[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\] \[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - p(A \cap B)\] \[P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(AB).\]

  • If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive—two events cannot occur simulatenously, then

    \[P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B)\]

    since $P(AB) = 0$ by definition.

  • Since $A$ and $A^\prime$ are mutually exclusive, we can apply this rule and have the following

    \[P(A^\prime) = 1 - P(A) \text{ and } P(A) = 1 - P(A^\prime).\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Roll a die. Find the probability of getting {3, 4} using addition rule.
Exercise 2: Suppose we have the following information:
  1. There is a 60% that John visits Hanoi.
  2. There is a 50% that John visits HCM City.
  3. There is a 30% that John visits both of the cities.
Find the probability that John visits either city.


Conditional Probability is the probability that A occurs given that B has already happened or the probability of action A based on a condition B. As such, event B happens first then event A happens. Imagine if you want to know whether there might be a rainbow tomorrow afternoon, it helps to know if it rains before then. The conditional probability is denoted and formulated as follows. We’ll discuss in detail the second equality in Bayes’ Rule.

\[P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(A)P(B | A)}{P(B)}\]

The first equality derives from probability definition. The condition “given B has already happened/a condition B” filters B in, saying that B is the new sample space. The condition “A occurs/action A” filters A in next, saying that from that sample space B, take only the ones from event A. The figure demonstrates this idea.

Let’s solve an example using both the idea and formula.

Statement Definition Formula
A fair six-sided die is rolled $\Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$  
A five is rolled $A = \{3\} \Rightarrow n(A) = 1$ $P(A) = \frac{1}{6}$
An odd number is rolled $B= \{1, 3, 5\} \Rightarrow n(B) = 3$ $P(B) = \frac{3}{6}$
Given B then A $n(AB) = 1$ $P(AB) = \frac{1}{6}$
Probability $P(A | B) = \frac{n(AB)}{n(B)} = \frac{1}{3}$ $P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{3}{6}} = \frac{1}{3}$


Multiplication Rule
For two events, we have the following

\[P(AB) = P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B | A) = P(B) \cdot P(A | B).\]

This formula is deduced from the conditional probability formula above,

\[P(A | B) = \frac{P(AB)}{P(B)} \text{ and } P(B | A) = \frac{P(AB)}{P(A)}\]

\begin{align} \label{conditional-multiplication} \Longrightarrow P(A) \cdot P(B | A) = P(AB) = P(B) \cdot P(A | B). \end{align}

In general, if all $A_i’s$ are true, we have the formula

\[P(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n) = \underbrace{\underbrace{P(A_1) \cdot P(A_2 | A_1)}_{P(A_1 A_2)} \cdot P(A_3 | A_1 A_2)}_{P(A_1 A_2 A_3)} \cdots P(A_n | A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n).\]

:pushpin: Pro tip: If we divide a problem into separate braches and handle them in a parallel manner, use additional rule. If a problem is a sequential events, use multiplication rule.

Example
Problem statement: There are 10 identical keys, two of which can open a door. Randomly pick and try each key without replacement---discarding it if it is unusable. What is the probability that the door is opened on the third attempt?
Breakdown:
  • without replacement
    • Event $A_1$ is to pick and try the first key which is right.
    • Event $A_2$ is to pick and try the second key which is right.
    • Event $A_3$ is to pick and try the third key which is right.
  • $P(A_1^\prime A_2^\prime A_3)$ is the desired probability.
Idea: We pick one unit from the pool of 10 and it is wrong. Then we pick another from the rest and it is wrong. We try the third time and it is correct.
  1. We pick one from 10 and it is wrong.
    • There are 2 correct keys out of 10, so $P(A_1) = \frac{2}{10}$.
    • Our chance of getting a wrong key is $P(A_1^\prime) = 1 - P(A_1) = 1 - \frac{2}{10} = \frac{8}{10}$.
  2. Discarding one wrong, we pick another from the rest and it is still wrong.
    • There are 10 in total and 1 was discarded, so we have 10 - 1 = 9 keys left.
    • There are still 2 correct keys, so so $P(A_2 | A_1^\prime) = \frac{2}{9}$ .
    • Our chance of getting another incorrect given one was removed is $P(A_2^\prime | A_1^\prime) = 1 - P(A_2 | A_1^\prime) = 1 - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{7}{9}$.
  3. Discard both wrong, we pick the third key from the rest and it can open the door.
    • There are 9 units left and 1 was removed, so we have 9 - 1 = 8 keys left.
    • There are 2 usable keys left and none has been picked, so we still 2 usuable keys in $A_3$.
    • Our chance of getting the first correct key given two were wrong is $P(A_3 | A_1^\prime A_2^\prime) = \frac{2}{8}$.
  4. $P(A_1^\prime A_2^\prime A_3) = \frac{8}{10} \cdot \frac{7}{9} \cdot \frac{2}{8} \approx 0.156$.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Find the probability of rolling an odd number given that it is a three.
Exercise 2: There are 10 identical keys, two of which can open a door. Randomly pick and try each key without replacement. What is the probability that the door is opened within at most three attempts?
Hints: At most three attempts means either one, two, or three attempts. Apply the additional rule.


Bayes’ Theorem

Total Probability Theorem

:question: Using conditional probability, we can find the likelihood of an event happening provided that another event is true. Now what if we want to find the probability of an event H and only know that several events have already occurred and they together make up the sample space?

We can divide this problem into two stages including

  • Stage 1 (choose the path you want to go with): events Ai are pairwise mutually exclusive and they combined are the sample space, which is called a complete system:
    • $A_i A_j = \emptyset$ $\forall i \neq j$
    • $\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i = A_1 + \cdots + A_n = \Omega$
    • $P(A_1) + \cdots + P(A_n) = 1$.
  • Stage 2 (take action according to the path): event H happens given that each Ai has already happened (each of them may or may not contain event H).

With this process and that all $A_i$ and $H_i = H \cap A_i$ happen separately, we’ll be able to obtain the desired probability. The idea is to divide event H into smaller events and handle each of them individually. You can think of $A_i \text{ and } H$ as variables, P(Ai) as coefficients and P(H) is the average with coefficients. The formula is as follows.

\[P(H) = P(H_1) + \cdots + P(H_n) = P(A_1) \cdot P(H | A_1) + \cdots + P(A_n) \cdot P(H | A_n)\] \[P(H) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A_i) \cdot P(H | A_i)\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: (Pick a Marble) There are three bags that each contain 100 marbles:
  • Bag 1 has 75 red and 25 blue marbles
  • Bag 2 has 60 red and 40 blue marbles
  • Bag 3 has 45 red and 55 blue marbles.
Choose one of the bags at random and then pick a marble from the chosen bag also randomly. What is the probability that the chosen marble is red?
Hints: Identify two main steps and draw a tree diagram.
Exercise 2: Use columns "Studied" and "Result" of the empirical table. Compute the probability that a student studied/didn't student given their result. Hint: Draw a tree diagram.


Bayes’ Rule

We can certainly pose another problem by reversing the situation from the Total Probability Theorem as follows.

:question: Suppose that the probability of $H$ as a whole is known. What is the probability of $A_i$ given $H$ is true?

Take the marble example; we know the probability of each color, how do we figure out which bag has more red marbles in terms of percentage? Now the problem becomes a conditional probability: What is the probability of picking a marble from bag 1/2/3 given that it is red?

Thus we can certainly use the result \eqref{conditional-multiplication} to obtain the following formula.

\[P(c | X) = \frac{P(X | c) \cdot P(c)}{P(X)}\]

where

  • Posterior $P(c | X)$ is the probability of c being true given X is true
  • Prior $P(c)$ is the probability of c (before carying X)
  • Likelihood $P(X | c)$ is the probability of X being true given c is true
  • Marginalization $P(X) \neq 0$ is the probability of X.

If $X$ is an event and $c$ is an element of a complete system ${C_1, \cdots, C_n}$ with $P(C_i) \neq 0$, then

\[P(C_i | X) = \frac{P(X | C_i) \cdot P(C_i)}{P(X)} = \frac{P(X | C_i) \cdot P(C_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(C_j) \cdot P(X | C_j)}.\]
Example
Problem statement (Pick a Marble): There are three bags that each contain 100 marbles:
  • Bag 1 has 75 red and 25 blue marbles
  • Bag 2 has 60 red and 40 blue marbles
  • Bag 3 has 45 red and 55 blue marbles.
Pick a random marble and it turns out to be red. What is the probability that it is from Bag 1?
Breakdown:
  • $X$ is the event of picking a red marble
  • $A_1$ is the event of the marble from bag 1
  • $A_2$ is the event of the marble from bag 2
  • $A_3$ is the event of the marble from bag 3
  • $P(A_1 | X) = \frac{P(X | A_1) \cdot P(A_1)}{P(X)}$ is the probability of a marble from bag 1 given it is red.
Idea: We can use answer from the previous exercises for $P(X)$. The numerator can also be computed using the tree diagram hint.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: (Detect Spam Email - Simple NLP Problem) Assume that the word ‘offer’ occurs in 80% of the spam messages in my account. Also, let’s assume ‘offer’ occurs in 10% of my desired e-mails. If 30% of the received e-mails are considered as a scam, and I will receive a new message which contains ‘offer’, what is the probability that it is spam?
Hint: Draw a tree diagram.
Exercise 2: Do you notice the pattern using a tree diagram to solve this kind of problem?
Exercise 3: (Simple Classification) Use columns "Studied" and "Result" of the empirical table. Compute the probability that a student passed student given their study status. Based on the probabilities, conclude if a student should study for the exam. Hint: Draw a tree diagram.
