Questions Answers
What does coefficient do in total probability? It is to evaluate the importance of each feature.
If H does not intersect with one of the Ai’s, can I exclude that Ai ? Yes. Then, P(Ai) = 0.
Besides tree diagram, are there any techniques I can use to solve Bayes-related problem? Yes. You can use confusion matrix for this matter.

entry.title: Math for AI 103 Warm-up
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on TA Nguyen Quoc Thai’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have known arithmetics or probability and statistics.

In today’s post, we’ll explore basic probability including Total Probability Theorem and Bayes’ Rule. We’ll go over some AI-related practice problems.

Basic Terminology

Defintions

Probability is the likehood of an event happening.

  • It is commonly expressed as a percentage $\%$ and ranges from $0$ to $1$ inclusively.
  • In daily life, we use words like “certain”, “likely”, “maybe” or “impossible” to express it.
  • $0$ is an impossible event and $1$ is a certain event.
  • For example, we say, “It’s unlikely to rain in the desert” or “It’s impossible for the sun to rise in the east.” The second statement mathematically means the probability of the sun rising in the east is 0.

An experiment is a planned operation through which specific results are obtained.

  • raining in the desert is an experiment
  • flipping a coin is an experiment.

An outcome is a result of an experiment. The sample space of an experiment is the set of all possible outcomes.

  • Possible outcomes are displayed within braces $\{\}$.
  • We can represent it in three following ways, which are demonstrated in later examples in this post,
    • list all possible outcomes
    • create a Venn diagram
    • create a tree diagram.

An event is a part/subset of the sample space. It can be any combination of outcomes.

Let’s take a look at some examples. Assume that the coin, die, and card deck are fair and regular.

Experiment Sample Space Event Probability
Flipping a coin {head, tail} {tail} $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = 50\%$
Rolling a die {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} {Die is even} = {2, 4, 6} $\frac{3}{6} = 0.5 = 50\%$
Picking a card out of a deck a set of 52 cards {Card is a club} = a set of 13 clubs $\frac{13}{52} = 0.25 = 25\%$


Relations of Events

Consider two events A and B from the same experiment.

Implication

  • Event A implies event B means if event A occurs, then event B occurs as well.
  • Mathematically, $A \Rightarrow B$ means $A \subseteq B$.

Equivalent

  • Event A equals event B means A implies B and B implies A.
  • Mathematically, $A \Rightarrow B$ and $B \Rightarrow A$ means $A \Leftrightarrow B$.

Operations on Events

Again, consider two events A and B from the same experiment. Then there are primary operations on them as follows.

Notation Operation Name Description
$A \cap B$ or $AB$ Intersection Both A and B happen
$A \cup B$ or $A + B$ Union Either A or B or both happen
$A^\complement$ or $A^\prime$ or $\overline{A}$ Complement A does not happen


The following example is solved by listing all possible outcomes in each event.

  Description Mathematical Result
Sample Space Rolling a die {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
Event A Rolling an even number {2, 4, 6}
Event B Rolling a number divisible by 3 {3, 6}
$AB$ Rolling a number that is even and divisible by 3 {6}
$A + B$ Rolling a number that is either even or divisible by 3 {2, 3, 4, 6}
$A^\prime$ Rolling a number that is not even {1, 3, 5}


Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Roll a die and A is an event of getting even sides. What is $A^\prime$?
Exercise 2: Roll a die. If A is an event of getting even sides and B is an event of getting a number greater than or equal to 4. What is $AB$?
Exercise 3: Roll a die. If A is an event of getting a number greater than 2 and B is an event of getting a number greater than or equal to 4. What is $A + B$?

Probability

There are two ways to describe probability formula: classical probability and geometric probability.

Classical Probability is represented by the formula

\[P(A) = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}} = \frac{n(A)}{n(\Omega)}.\]

We’ll use the same event A from the above experiment and have

  • $\Omega = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \} \Rightarrow n_{\Omega} = 6$
  • $A = \{ 2, 4, 6 \} \Rightarrow n_{A} = 3$
  • $P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(\Omega)} = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 = 50\%$.

Geometric Probability

\[P(A) = \frac{\text{measure of domain A}}{\text{measure of domain } \Omega}\]

where domain is the region an event can be.

While length measures the region in 1D, area measures the region in 2D. We’ll go over an example in one dimension.

Let $x$ an arbitrary real number between 0 and 3 inclusively. What is the probability of $x$ closer to 0 than 1?

  • Breakdown: Only numbers less than 0.5 are closer to 0 than 1. That is the region where $x$ can be to satisfy the condition.
  • $A = (0, 0.5) \Rightarrow \text{measure of domain A} = \text{length of segment } (0, 0.5) = 0.5$
  • $\Omega = (0, 3) \Rightarrow \text{measure of domain } \Omega = \text{length of segment } (0, 3) = 3$
  • $P(A) = \frac{\text{measure of domain A}}{\text{measure of domain } \Omega} = \frac{0.5}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: What is the probability of picking a heart from a 52-card deck?
Exercise 2: There are 3 red marbles and 2 green marbles. What is the probability of getting a red one?
Exercise 3: Assume $x$ selected from the set ${-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}$. What is the probability of $x^2 > 0$?
Exercise 4: Roll 2 dice. What is the probability of getting two sides summed up to 5?
Exercise 5: Using the 1D geometric probability example, what is the probability if x is closer to $2.5$ than $1$?
Exercise 6: A dart is thrown at a circular dartboard such that it will land randomly on the area of the dartboard. What is the probability of it landing closer to the center "Success" than to the edge?


Rules of Probability

Addition Rule refers to the probability of at least one event happening.

  • Generally, we have

    \[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\] \[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - p(A \cap B)\] \[P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(AB).\]

  • If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive—two events cannot occur simulatenously, then

    \[P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B)\]

    since $P(AB) = 0$ by definition.

  • Since $A$ and $A^\prime$ are mutually exclusive, we can apply this rule and have the following

    \[P(A^\prime) = 1 - P(A) \text{ and } P(A) = 1 - P(A^\prime).\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Find the probability of getting 1 or 5 when rolling a fair six-sided die.
Exercise 2: Find the probability of getting a number different from 1 and 6 when rolling a fair six-sided die.


Conditional Probability is the probability that A occurs given that B has already happened. Imagine if you want to know whether there might be a rainbow tomorrow afternoon, it helps to know if it rains before then. The conditional probability is denoted and formulated as follows. We’ll discuss in detail the second equality in Bayes’ Rule.

\[P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(A)P(B | A)}{P(B)}\]

The first equality derives from probability definition. The condition “given B has already happened” says that all the possible outcomes are from event B. The condition “A occurs” says that from those outcomes, take only the ones from event A. The figure demonstrates this idea.

Let’s solve an example using both the idea and formula.

Statement Definition Formula
A fair six-sided die is rolled $\Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$  
A five is rolled $A = \{5\} \Rightarrow n(A) = 1$ $P(A) = \frac{1}{6}$
An odd number is rolled $B= \{1, 3, 5\} \Rightarrow n(B) = 3$ $P(B) = \frac{3}{6}$
Given B then A $n(AB) = 1$ $P(AB) = \frac{1}{6}$
Probability $P(A | B) = \frac{n(AB)}{n(B)} = \frac{1}{3}$ $P(A | B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{\frac{1}{6}}{\frac{3}{6}} = \frac{1}{3}$


Multiplication Rule
From the conditional probability formula, we can deduce a formula for two events. The formula for a general case is provided below and will be explained in Math for AI 103.

\[P(AB) = P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B | A) = P(B) \cdot P(A | B)\] \[P(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n) = P(A_1) \cdot P(A_2 | A_1) \cdot P(A_3 | A_1 A_2) \cdots P(A_n | A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n)\]

Let’s first see how conditional probability formula implies the first formula here and then take an example to see how these formulae work.

\[P(A \\| B) = \frac{P(AB)}{P(B)} \text{ and } P(B \\| A) = \frac{P(AB)}{P(A)}\]

\begin{align} \label{conditional-multiplication} \Longrightarrow P(A) \cdot P(B | A) = P(AB) = P(B) \cdot P(A | B) \end{align}

Example
Problem statement: In a factory, there are 100 units of a certain product, five of which are defective. Pick three units at once/without replacement. What is the probability that none of them are defective?
Breakdown:
  • at once means together in one time
  • without replacement means one after another and not returning to the original pool.
    • Event $A_1$ is to pick the first non-defective unit.
    • Event $A_2$ is to pick the second non-defective unit.
    • Event $A_3$ is to pick the last non-defective unit.
  • Both approaches give the same result because three distinct items are chosen from the same fixed population and the order of selection does not matter.
Idea: The problem can be approached differently depending on the terminology and we'll go with without replacement in this solution. We pick one unit from the pool of 100 and hope it is non-defective. Then we pick another from the rest and hope the same thing. We repeat this one more time.
  1. We pick one from 100 and hope it is non-defective.
    • There are five defectives out of 100, so there are 100 - 5 = 95 non-defectives in $A_1$.
    • Our chance of getting a non-defective is $P(A_1) = \frac{95}{100}$.
  2. Given that the first selected product was good, we pick another from the rest and hope it is non-defective.
    • There are 100 in total and 1 was picked, so we have 100 - 1 = 99 units left.
    • There are 95 non-defectives in total and 1 was assumed to be picked, so we have 95 - 1 = 94 non-defective units left in $A_2$.
    • Our chance of getting another non-defective given one has already been picked is $P(A_2 | A_1) = \frac{94}{99}$.
  3. Given that both selected items were fine, we pick the last unit from the rest and hope it is non-defective.
    • There are 99 units left and 1 was picked, so we have 99 - 1 = 98 units left.
    • There are 94 non-defectives left and 1 was assumed to be picked, so we have 94 - 1 = 93 non-defective units in $A_3$ now.
    • Our chance of getting another non-defective is $P(A_3 | A_1 A_2) = \frac{93}{98}$.
  4. $P(A_1 A_2 A_3) = \frac{95}{100} \cdot \frac{94}{99} \cdot \frac{93}{98} \approx 0.856$.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Find the probability of rolling an odd number given that it is a five.
Exercise 2: Suppose you pick a card from a standard deck. Find the probability of getting a J, Q, and K if we know that card is red.
Exercise 2: Suppose you take out two cards from a standard deck of cards one after another without replacement. What is the probability that the first is the ace of spade and the second if a heart?


Total Probability Theorem

:question: Using conditional probability, we can find the likelihood of an event happening provided that another event is true. Now what if we want to find the probability of an event H and only know that several events have already occurred and they together make up the sample space?

We can divide this problem into two stages including

  • Stage 1: events $A_i$ are pairwise mutually exclusive and they combined are the sample space, which is called a complete system:
    • $A_i A_j = \emptyset$ $\forall i \neq j$
    • $\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i = A_1 + \cdots + A_n = \Omega$
    • $P(A_1) + \cdots + P(A_n) = 1$.
  • Stage 2: event $H$ happens given that each $A_i$ has already happened (each of them may or may not contain event H).

With this process and that $A_i$ and $H_i = H \cap A_i$ happen separately, we’ll be able to obtain the desired probability. The idea is to divide event $H$ into smaller events and handle each of them. The formula for this idea is as follows.

\[P(H) = P(H_1) + \cdots + P(H_n) = P(A_1) \cdot P(H | A_1) + \cdots + P(A_n) \cdot P(H | A_n)\] \[P(H) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A_i) \cdot P(H | A_i)\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: (Widget Dectection) Company M supplies 80% of widgets for a car shop and only 1% of their widgets turn out to be defective. Company N supplies the remaining 20% of widgets for the car shop and 3% of their widgets turn out to be defective. If a customer randomly purchases a widget from the car shop, what is the probability that it will be defective?
Hints: Complete the tree diagram below and apply the formula. Exercise 2: (Pick a Marble) There are three bags that each contain 100 marbles:
  • Bag 1 has 75 red and 25 blue marbles
  • Bag 2 has 60 red and 40 blue marbles
  • Bag 3 has 45 red and 55 blue marbles.
Choose one of the bags at random and then pick a marble from the chosen bag also randomly. What is the probability that the chosen marble is red?
Hint: Draw a tree diagram as above.


Bayes’ Rule

We can certainly pose another problem by reversing the situation from the Total Probability Theorem as follows.

:question: Suppose that the probability of $H$ as a whole is known. What is the probability of $A_i$ given $H$ is true?

Take the car shop example; we know the probability of defective units, how do we figure out which company provides more defective products in terms of percentage? Now the problem becomes a conditional probability: What is the probability of a product coming from each company given that the product is defective?

Thus we can certainly use the result \eqref{conditional-multiplication} to obtain the following formula.

\[P(c | X) = \frac{P(X | c) \cdot P(c)}{P(X)}\]

where

  • Posterior $P(c | X)$ is the probability of c being true given X is true
  • Prior $P(c)$ is the probability of c
  • Likelihood $P(X | c)$ is the probability of X being true given c is true
  • Marginalization $P(X)$ is the probability of X.

If c is an element of a complete system ${A_1, \cdots, A_n}$ and X is an event $H$ with $P(A_i) \neq 0$, then

\[P(A_i | H) = \frac{P(H | A_i) \cdot P(A_i)}{P(H)} = \frac{P(H | A_i) \cdot P(A_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A_j) \cdot P(H | A_j)}.\]
Example
Problem statement: (Widget Detection) Company M supplies 80% of widgets for a car shop and only 1% of their widgets turn out to be defective. Company N supplies the remaining 20% of widgets for the car shop and 3% of their widgets turn out to be defective. If a customer randomly purchases a widget from the car shop and it turns out to be defective, what is the probability of the product from company M?
Breakdown:
  • $H$ is the event of a unit being defective
  • $M$ is the event of a unit from company M
  • $N$ is the event of a unit from company N
  • $P(M | H) = \frac{P(H | M) \cdot P(M)}{P(H)}$ is the probability of a unit from M given it is defective.
Idea: We can use answer from the previous exercises for $P(H)$. The numerator can also be computed using the tree diagram hint.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: (Widget Detection) Complete the above example. Find the probability of a product from company N such that it is defective. Which company provides more defective units in terms of percentage?
Exercise 2: (Pick a Marble) Use the marble example from previous exercises. Pick a random marble and it turns out to be red. What is the probability that it is from Bag 1?
Exercise 3: (Detect Spam Email - Simple NLP Problem) Assume that the word ‘offer’ occurs in 80% of the spam messages in my account. Also, let’s assume ‘offer’ occurs in 10% of my desired e-mails. If 30% of the received e-mails are considered as a scam, and I will receive a new message which contains ‘offer’, what is the probability that it is spam?
Hint: Draw a tree diagram.
Exercise 4: Do you notice the pattern using a tree diagram to solve this kind of problem?
Exercise 5: A card is lost from a pack of 52 cards. From the remaining cards two are drawn randomly and found to be both clubs. Find the probability that the lost card is also a clubs.
Hints: Draw a tree diagram. The given condition is that two cards are drawn at random.
Exercise 6: Solve exercise 5 in a one-line argument.
Hints: Use only logic and definition of probability.

entry.title: Math for AI 102
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read Math for AI 101, had some coding experience, and known a bit of AI knowledge. Absolute beginners are encouraged to read the material and repeatedly practice coding without AI assistance to strengthen their coding and code-reading skills. Note that only necessary Python knowledge is introduced here. Also, not every single detail from Linear Algebra is introduced in this Math for AI series. Instead, we’ll learn pick up more material along the way.

The simplest ideas reveal what is most essential and enduring.
-Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh

In today’s post, we’ll explore matrices and cosine similarity. We’ll also discuss some applications in AI including background substraction, traffic sign matching, and K-nearest neighbors.

All data can be transformed into vectors, so Linear Algebra can handle most of the real-world information.

Vector and Matrix

A vector is a collection of real numbers and has a length of n, that is, \(\mathbf{u} = \vec{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

A matrix is a collection/generalization of vectors and has m rows and n columns, that is, \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} &\cdots& a_{1n} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ a_{m1} &\cdots& a_{mn} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\).

Mathematically, a linear equation is an equation where the variables/unknowns’ power is at most one. Its graph for one variable is called a line, for two variables is a plane, and for more than two is a hyperplane. For example, if $x_1, \cdots, x_n$ are variables, then some linear equations are

\[\begin{align*} y &= a x + b \\ y &= a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + b \\ y &= a_1 x_1 \cdots a_n x_n + b. \end{align*}\]

System of Linear Equations

Assume that a company’s sales depends on their advertising expenses on TV, radio, and newspaper and specifically computed based on the linear equation formula

\[\begin{align*} S &= a_1 T + a_2 R + a_3 N &+ b \\ \text{Sales } &= a_1 \text{TV} + a_2 \text{Radio} + a_3 \text{Newspaper} &+ b \end{align*}\]

where $a_1, a_2, a_3, \text{ and } b$ are fixed for specific sets of T, R, and N. If we know all these parameters and expenses, we can easily figure out S.

For the sake of simplicity, we can exclude b or set b to be 0. If there are three sets of T, R, N, and S, we can construct a system of linear equations

\[\begin{align*} a_1 T_1 + a_2 R_1 + a_3 N_1 = S_1 \\ a_1 T_2 + a_2 R_2 + a_3 N_2 = S_2 \\ a_1 T_3 + a_2 R_3 + a_3 N_3 = S_3. \end{align*}\]

We can also rewrite this system using vectors

\[a_1 \begin{bmatrix} T_1 \\ R_1 \\ N_1 \end{bmatrix} + a_2 \begin{bmatrix} T_2 \\ R_2 \\ N_2 \end{bmatrix} + a_3 \begin{bmatrix} T_3 \\ R_3 \\ N_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} S_1 \\ S_2 \\ S_3 \end{bmatrix}\]

and matrix

\[\begin{bmatrix} T_1 & R_1 & N_1 \\ T_2 & R_2 & N_2 \\ T_3 & R_3 & N_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \\ a_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} S_1 \\ S_2 \\ S_3 \end{bmatrix}.\]

For this matrix-vector calculation, each linear equation or each entry in the resulting vector is obtained by multiplying the corresponding row of the matrix with the vector and summing the results. Each multiplication is known as dot product, which will be introduced later.

Generally, we can have more unknowns $a_i’s$ than equations or vice versa and, regardless of circumstance, write

\[A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\]

where $A$ is a data matrix, $\mathbf{x}$ is an unknown, $\mathbf{b}$ is a data vector, and the number of columns in $A$ must match that of the unknown vector $\mathbf{x}$.

If we have more unknowns than equations, then there are infinitely many solutions. In such cases, our goal is to figure out the most optimized solution.

Vectors Operations

For scalar $\alpha$, \(\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\), we have the following vector operations.

Operation Formula Commutative
Vector Addition
  • element-wise addition
  • $+$
  • np.add(vec1, vec2)
  • np.add(vec2, vec1)
$$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 + v_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n + v_n \end{bmatrix}$$ $$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}$$
Vector Subtraction
  • element-wise subtraction
  • $-$
  • np.subtract(vec1, vec2)
$$\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 - v_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n - v_n \end{bmatrix}$$ :x:
Hadamard Product
  • element-wise multiplication
  • $*$
  • np.multiply(vec1, vec2)
  • np.multiply(vec2, vec1)
$$\mathbf{u} \odot \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 v_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n v_n \end{bmatrix}$$ $$\mathbf{u} \odot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{u}$$
Hadamard Division
  • element-wise division
  • $/$
  • np.divide(vec1, vec2)
$$\mathbf{u} \oslash \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 / v_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n / v_n \end{bmatrix}$$ :x:
Scalar Multiplication
  • $*$
$$\alpha \mathbf{u} = \alpha \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha u_1 \\ \vdots \\ \alpha u_n \end{bmatrix}$$ $$\alpha \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u} \alpha$$
Transpose
  • convert rows into columns
  • vec.T
$$\mathbf{u}^\intercal = [u_1 \cdots u_n] \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}$$ :x:
Dot Product
  • np.dot(vec1, vec2)
  • np.dot(vec2, vec1)
  • vec1.subtract(vec2)
  • vec2.subtract(vec1)
$$\begin{align*} &\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \mathbf{u}^\intercal \mathbf{v} \\ &= u_1 \times v_1 + \cdots + \ u_n \times v_n \end{align*}$$ $$\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$$
Norm/Length of a Vector
  • np.linalg.norm(vec)
  • normally use squared norm $\left \lVert \mathbf{u} \right \rVert ^2$
$$\begin{align*} &\left \lVert \mathbf{u} \right \rVert = \sqrt{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}} \\ &= \sqrt{u_1^2 + \cdots u_n^2} \end{align*}$$ :x:


Geometrically, dot product of two vectors is based on the projection of the first vector onto the second, that is, represent how much the former points in the same direction as the latter. The more positive and higher the result is, the more similar directions they point towards and vice versa. If the result is 0, then two vectors are perpendiclar/orthogonal.

Matrix Operations

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} &\cdots& a_{1n} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ a_{m1} &\cdots& a_{mn} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} b_{11} &\cdots& b_{1q} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ b_{p1} &\cdots& b_{pq} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}\), and \(\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\), we have the following operations.

Operation Formula Commutative
Matrix Addition
  • element-wise addition
For $m = p$ and $n = q$, $$A + B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} + b_{11} &\cdots& a_{1n} + b_{1q} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ a_{m1} + b_{p1} &\cdots& a_{mn} + b_{pq} \end{bmatrix}$$ $$A + B = B + A$$
Vector Subtraction
  • element-wise subtraction
For $m = p$ and $n = q$, $$A - B = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} - b_{11} &\cdots& a_{1n} - b_{1q} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ a_{m1} - b_{p1} &\cdots& a_{mn} - b_{pq} \end{bmatrix}$$ :x:
Transpose
  • convert rows into columns
  • mat.T
$$A^\intercal = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} &\cdots& a_{m1} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ a_{1n} &\cdots& a_{mn} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$$ :x:
Matrix-Vector Multiplication
  • transform a vector using a matrix
  • np.dot(mat, vec)
  • mat @ vec
  • mat.dot(vec)
$$\mathbf{c} = A \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} x_1 + \cdots + a_{1n} x_n \\ \vdots \\ a_{m1} x_1 + \cdots + a_{mn} x_n \end{bmatrix}$$ $$c \in \mathbb{R}^m \text{ where } c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} x_j$$ :x:
Matrix-Matrix Multiplication
  • transformations at once
  • np.dot(mat1, mat2)
  • mat1 @ mat2
  • mat1.dot(mat2)
For $n = p$, $$\begin{align*} &C = AB \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} \sum_{j=1}^n a_{1j} b_{j1} &\cdots& \sum_{j=1}^n a_{1j} b_{jq} \\ \vdots &\ddots& \vdots \\ \sum_{j=1}^n a_{mj} b_{j1} &\cdots& \sum_{j=1}^n a_{mj} b_{jq} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}$$ $$C \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times q} \text{ where } c_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} b_{jk}$$ :x:


Notation and Other Operations
$X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is also denoted by $X \sim (m, n)$. This is also applied to higher-dimensional matrices.

We can also take exponential function or square root of a matrix as follows.

x = np.arange(6).reshape((2,3))
print(f'x is {x}')
print(f'square root of x is {np.sqrt(x)}')
print(f'exponential of x is {np.exp(x)}')

'''
x is [[0 1 2]
      [3 4 5]]
square root of x is [[0.         1.         1.41421356]
                     [1.73205081 2.         2.23606798]]
exponential of x is [[  1.           2.71828183   7.3890561 ]
                     [ 20.08553692  54.59815003 148.4131591 ]]
'''

argmin and argmax
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be and array and $D$ be its elements’ indices.

  min max
np.min()
np.max()
get the value		 $\{x_i \in \mathbf{x} | x_i \le x_j \forall x_j \in \mathbf{x} \}$ $\{x_i \in \mathbf{x} | x_i \ge x_j \forall x_j \in \mathbb{x} \}$
np.argmin()
np.argmax()
get the index		 $\{i \in D | x_i \le x_j \forall x_j \in \mathbf{x} \}$ $\{x_i \in D | x_i \ge x_j \forall x_j \in \mathbf{x} \}$


Summation and Average
We use np.sum() and np.mean() to compute the summation and average of values of a vector. The mathematical formulae for these methods are as follows.

\[sum(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i} x_i\] \[average(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i} x_i\]
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Given x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) and y = np.array([5, 6, 7, 8]), write code for vector operations using NumPy.
Exercise 2: Consider vectors in exercise 1 as lists, use zip() to write code for vector operations above.
Exercise 3: For exercise 1, write code for norm of a vector without using the suggested method.
Exercise 4: Given x = np.array([[4, 2], [9, 8]]) and y = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), write code for matrix operations using NumPy.
Exercise 5: Explain the third equality in the dot product formula in vector operations.
Exercise 6: Given u = [1, 12, 20, 2] is a vector, what is $\frac{\mathbf{u}}{\left \lVert \mathbf{u} \right \rVert}$?
Exercise 7: If $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$, which of the following is valid?
  • $AB$
  • $BA$
  • $A^\intercal B$
  • $AB^\intercal$
Exercise 8: Which of the following compute sum of elements of x = np.array([1, 4, 3])?
  • np.dot(x, x)
  • np.sqrt(np.dot(x, x))
  • np.dot(x, y) where y = np.ones_like(x)


:bulb: Applications in AI

We know from the previous post that

  • a color image is a 3D matrix of values between 0 and 255, (Height, Width, channel) where there are 3 color channels RGB
  • a grayscale image is a 2D matrix of values between 0 and 255, (Height, Width).

Rotate Left an Image (Perpendicular)
We’ve learned how to handle a 2D matrix above, so rotating left a grayscale image should be feasible just using some above operations.

About the case of a color image—a 3D matrix, we know the last dimension is always 3 since it contains color channels. But we do want to swap its height and width. We can certainly do this using the idea of array indexing. The hint is that we can use the NumPy method np.transpose().

Convert Color to Grayscale Image

Example: Image Color Conversion
Problem statement: Convert a color image into a grayscale image.
Breakdown: Broadcasting and Matrix-Vector Multiplication $A \mathbf{x}$
  • Broadcasting can stretch a vector to be suitable for an operation.
  • The multiplication can change the shape of the matrix.
  • The resulting "vector" is obtained by multiplying the elements of each row of the matrix with the corresponding elements of the vector and summing such results.
  • The original vector acts as weights/coefficients of each row of the matrix.
Idea: To perform this conversion, we want to exterminate the last dimension. If we think of the color matrix, what we want is to suppress three channels into one in a sense that the values are still in the range from 0 to 255.
  1. Solution 1: Take their mean (without np.mean())
    2. The mean of three numbers is calculated as their sum divided by three. As such the weight for each number is $\frac{1}{3}$. Then, we can use matrix-vector multiplication on the color image and $vector = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}$ to create a grayscale image.
  2. Solution 2: Use standard ratio
    3. The standard ratio for color-grayscale is $[R, G, B] = [0.213, 0.715, 0.072]$. Using this ratio, we can also create a vector and apply the matrix-vector multiplication on it and a color image.
    :warning: OpenCV reads a color image in order BGR, not RGB.


In fact, OpenCV provides a function that can convert a color to grayscale image. The example above demonstrates behind-the-scene computation.

color_image = cv2.cvtColor(color_image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

Background Subtraction
In OpenCV, there is a function called cv2.threshold(), which works quite similarly to np.clip() or np.where() in NumPy. This function is specifically used for image data, not ndarray in general. Be mindful about the proper data type that it can handle.

import cv2

_, array_output = cv2.threshold(array_input, threshold, max_value, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

This statement returns two outputs including the threshold and the thresholded image known as mask, respectively. Note that the threshold and max_value are numbers but need not be integers. According to THRESH_BINARY, we can interpret the condition statement that

\[\begin{equation*} output\_values = \begin{cases} max\_value &\text{if } input\_value > threshold \\ 0 &\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation*}\]
Example: Background Subtraction
Problem statement: We want to place a foreground image into a fake background provided that the placement region in the fake background is erased before we place it.
Breakdown: Consider three input images and one output image as follows.
  • Background B: the original background without the object.
  • Fake Background F: the background that we want to place the object on.
  • Input Image I: the image with the original background and object on it.
  • Output Image O: the image with the fake background and object on it.
Idea: We first need to get the object out of the original background. Then we can place it on the fake background.
  1. Any image is a matrix of values between 0 (black) and 255 (white), so we can do matrix operations on it.
  2. Matrix operations only work when matrices are proper in the situation. So we need to make sure our image matrices are of the same size.
  3. Get the object out of the original background by taking absolute difference.
    • We can separate the object and B in I by creating a clear distinction between them. Since the only difference between B and I is the object area, we can take their difference.
    • Taking the difference only might result in negative values since the background can be darker than the object itself. So we instead take the absolute difference.
    • As such the duplicated parts result in 0, practically close to 0 due to external factors like lighting.
    We need to make values close to 0 become exactly 0 so we have the resulting image which is called foreground mask.
  4. Place the object on the fake background.
    • If the foreground mask is 0, O takes F's values.
    • If the foreground mask is 255, O takes I's values.
    Once we apply these conditions, we will obtain O.
  5. We can improve this solution.
    • We replace the absolute difference values with their (weighted) average along the color channel dimension.
    • As such, image positions being 0 on all three channels (black) are replaced with F's values.
    • Image positions being 0 on fewer than three channels are replaced with I's values.
    This technique is applied to avoid values from both F and I are mixed up.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Write code for the color-grayscale conversion problem (both solutions).
Exercise 2: Write code to rotate left a grayscale image using both matrix operation and NumPy method and a color image using NumPy method.
Exercise 3: Try cv2.threshold() with an arbitrary array.
Exercise 4: In the second step of background subtraction problem, provide a situation where the difference is negative.
Exercise 5: Write code for background subtraction problem using arbitrary images (two versions).

Cosine Similarity

A loss function is a part of the model training process and cosine similarity can be used for such functions.

Dot Product

In addition to length/norm, a vector is always associated with only one direction. Two vectors can have similar or different directions. For example, scale of a vector have different length but the same direction as itself. Practically, we can think words like teachers, students, and banks. The first two may be arranged in relevant categories, so their vectors may point in closer directions. On the other hand, the last two may not.

DEMONSTRATION 3-4 images

As mentioned previously, dot product of two vectors is geometrically based on the projection of one vector onto another. This contributes to the geometric definition in the table below. Figure ? illustrates

  • the smaller the angle between two vectors is
  • the closer they are
  • the longer the projection of one vector onto the other is
  • the more they points in the same direction.

If the result is negative, their directions are different or opposite. If it is positive, they are similar or the same. If it is 0, they are perpendicular. Therefore, dot product actually represents how much one vector points in the same direction as the other. This refers to the similarity of two vectors, which goes together with cosine similarity. In fact, the definition of dot product between two vectors involves the cosine of their smaller angle.

Algebraic Geometric
\(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i\) \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \left \lVert \mathbf{u} \right \rVert \cos{(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})} \left \lVert \mathbf{v} \right \rVert\)


Cosine Similarity

Cosine similarity is used to measure the similarity between two vectors. From two definitions above, we have the formula for cosine of the smaller angle between two vectors

\[\cos(\alpha) = \cos{(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\left \lVert \mathbf{u} \right \rVert \left \lVert \mathbf{v} \right \rVert} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2}} \in [-1, 1].\]

Three important property for $\cos(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$ are

  1. The more similar two vectors are, the closer to 1 $\cos(\alpha)$ is
  2. $\cos(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \cos(a \mathbf{u}, b \mathbf{v}) \text{ for } ab > 0$
  3. $\cos(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) \neq \cos(\mathbf{u} + c, \mathbf{v} + d)$.

Above we have an example of words that shows usefulness of cosine similarity. Moreover, this concept can be applied to spot similar images.

  • We know that we can use basic operations to change brightness of an image.
  • Obviously, images with different brightness are still the same.
  • If we use absolute difference on them, a computer will distinguish them as dissimilar.
  • Using cosine similarity can address this issue thanks to the second property.
Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Prove two definitions of dot product are equivalent.
Hints: Use cosine formula in a triangle. Use vector formula for sides in a triangle. Use squared norm instead of norm.
Exercise 2: Prove the second property. Give an example for the third.
Exercise 3: Write code to compute dot product using the geometric definition.
Exercise 4: Write code to compute cosine similarity between two vectors using zip() and NumPy.
Exercise 5: Given u = [1, 1], which of the following vector is the most similar to u?
  • n = [-2, 1]
  • k = [-2, -1]
  • m = [2, -1]
  • r = [2, 1]
Exercise 6: Given the following, compute cosine between x and y and between u and v.

:bulb: Applications in AI

A unit vector is a vector of length 1. The unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{x}$ is the vector $\frac{\mathbf{x}}{\left \lVert \mathbf{x} \right \rVert}$.

The distance between two points $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the length of the vector from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$.

\[dist(x,y) = \left \lVert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x} \right \rVert.\]

While the absolute difference of two vectors is a vector, the distance between their heads (two points) is the length/norm of the resulting vector.

Traffic Sign Matching

One real-world application for absolute difference, distance, and cosine similarity is checking if two traffic signs are similar or not. They are similar when

  1. Absolute difference and distance are small and close to 0
    • Issue: The flip of an image is concluded to be more similar than its brighter image. This is because the results for the former may be smaller than that for the latter.
  2. Cosine similarity is close to 1.
    • Address the Issue: The brightness of an image has no significant effect on images’ similarity.

Figures below demonstrates the problem with absolute difference and distance and a solution using cosine similarity.

:question: What if two images are the same but one is a rotation of the other?

K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

KNN is a popular algorithm in Machine Learning. It involves considering each piece of data as a vector and computing the distance between a testing point and training points. As such, the algorithm can select the K nearest neighbors and make further analysis to provide an suitable ouput.

Practice Exercises
Exercise 1: Write code to compute absolute difference, distance, and cosine similarity.
Exercise 2: From exercise 1, which pair of signs has the lowest absolute difference/distance? Do they also have the highest or lowest cosine similarity?

:speech_balloon: FAQ

Here are some good questions asked during class. The answers to these questions came from either some admin, TA, STA, or members of AIO2025.

Questions Answers
Resources https://textbooks.math.gatech.edu/ila/index.html
What are other practical use of cosine similarity? NLP, Classification, Film Recommendation, Plagarism checker or budget control and sales prediction.
Should I use cosine similarity to preprocess image data to eliminate external factors? No. Other common functions to deal iwth external factors are Gaussian blurring or median filtering.

entry.title: Math for AI 101
entry.content:
Acknowledgement: This post is based mainly on Dr. Quang-Vinh Dinh’s presentation and slides and partly on on TA, STA, and peers’ responses from the course AIO2025 offered by AI VIETNAM.

Relevance: The audience of this lecture were those who have read Python for AI 106, had some coding experience, and known a bit of AI knowledge. Absolute beginners are encouraged to read the material and repeatedly practice coding without AI assistance to strengthen their coding and code-reading skills. Note that only necessary Python knowledge is introduced here. Also, not every single detail from Linear Algebra is introduced in this Math for AI series. Instead, we’ll learn pick up more material along the way.

In today’s post, we’ll explore Numpy. We’ll also discuss some applications in AI including Image Brightness with OpenCV.

NumPy

To create and use an array in NumPy, we must include a numpy package with the following syntax

import numpy as np

NumPy Array

Numpy is a standard Python library commonly used for numerical computing. The core object in NumPy is ndarray which is a multi-dimensional array data structure. NumPy can interact with various libraries and frameworks. We’ll refer to a NumPy array as an array from now on unless stated otherwise.

Purpose Frameworks and Libraries
Machine Learning - Deep Learning TensorFlow, PyTorch, Keras, scikit learn
Natural Language Processing Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK), GENSIM, spaCy
Scientific Computing Pandas
Visualization matplotlib, plotly


:question: Lists can work with multi-dimensional data structures. What else do we need for?

A list is ideal for storing one-dimensional data, but it is rather confusing when representing and handling multi-dimensional data due to its flexibility and slow performance. NumPy was created to address these issues. With NumPy, programmers need not write custom functions for common operations like squaring elements—built-in computational methods handle them efficiently. Basically, NumPy is a streamlined library.

  • Execution view: The operation is automatically applied to every selected element in the array.
  • Implementation view: We write the code as if it is performed on a single element.

The fact that Python lists can be inconsistent in how they are nested makes it difficult to define a clear sense of dimension or shape like we can with arrays. For an array, we can extract such information using built-in methods shape or ndim.

arr_1D = np.array([1, 2])
arr_1D
>>> [1 2]
arr_1D.shape
>>> (2, )
arr_1D.ndim
>>> 1

arr_2D = np.reshape((2,1))
arr_2D
>>> [[1]
     [2]]
arr_2D.shape
>>> (2, 1)
arr_2D.ndim
>>> 2

It is imperative to note that a column matrix is different from a vector in NumPy even though they basically are \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), which is totally different from in Mathematics.

a = np.array([[1, 2, 7, 3], [3, 4, 8, 5], [5, 6, 9, 4]])
# 2D nested array 
a.ndim
>>> 2
# 3-by-4 matrix
a.shape
>>> (3, 4)

Note that the term “dimension” and “axis” are interchangeable with arrays. For example, a one-dimensional array (1D) has one axis, a two-dimensional array (2D) has two axes, a three-dimensional array (3D) has three axes, and so on. The number of elements along each axis determines the shape of an array. Each axis has its own default direction, for instance,

  • Axis 0: from top to bottom (rows)
  • Axis 1: from left to right (columns)
  • Axis 2: from front to back (depth).

Some Common Methods

When learning a concept in coding, it’s imperative we know how to create it. There are a few ways to make an array either from scratch or from a pre-exiting array.

Create a NumPy Array (from scratch)
We can

  • convert a list into an array (demonstrated above)
  • make an array of a desired shape with zeros/ones via np.zeros() or np.ones()
  • produce an equally-spaced array using np.arange().

Note that numpy arrays are displayed without commas in the output.

import numpy as np

# an_np_array = np.array(python_list)
list1D = [1, 2, 3]
array1D = np.array(list1D)
print(f'array1D from list1D is {array1D}')

# np.zeros(tuple)
zeros_array = np.zeros((2,3))
print(f'zeros_array is {zeros_array}')

# np.ones(tuple)
ones_array = np.ones((2,3))
print(f'ones_array is {ones_array}')

# np.arange(start, end, step)
range_array_1 = np.arange(5)
range_array_2 = np.arange(0, 5, 0.5)
print(f'range of 5 is {range_array_1}')
print(f'range with step is {range_array_2}')

'''
array1D from list1D is [1 2 3]
zeros_array is [[0. 0. 0.]
                [0. 0. 0.]]
ones_array is [[1. 1. 1.]
                [1. 1. 1.]]
range of 5 is [0 1 2 3 4]
range with step is [0.  0.5 1.  1.5 2.  2.5 3.  3.5 4.  4.5]
'''

We can certainly make an array of any number by multiplying an array with only ones by that number. This is one simple example of execution-implementation views previously mentioned. This idea will be introduced in the Broadcasting section.

Create a NumPy Array (from an pre-existing array)

  • Each array has its own shape as we saw earlier, but such a shape isn’t fixed but can rather be reasonably modified using np.reshape(), reshape(), or flatten(). These methods operate from left to right and from top to bottom. While flatten() transforms any array into a 1D or vector, the other two are more flexible. However, we can only turn an array into a shape in which the number of elements stays unchanged.

For future references, flatten() is utilized in CNNs and Transformers.

import numpy as np

# np.reshape(an_array, new_shape_tuple)
data = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4], [4, 5, 6, 7], [7, 8, 9, 0]])
data_rs_1 = np.reshape(data, (2,6))
data_rs_1
>>> [[1 2 3 4 4 5]
     [6 7 7 8 9 0]]

# an_array.reshape(new_shape_tuple)
data_rs_2 = data.reshape((4,-1))
data_rs_2
>>> [[1 2 3]
     [4 4 5]
     [6 7 7]
     [8 9 0]]

# an_array.flatten()
data_rs_3 = data.flatten()
data_rs_3
>>> [1 2 3 4 4 5 6 7 7 8 9 0]

From the example above, notice that one dimension can be stated with some negative number as long as all others are specified when reshaping an array.

  • Another commonly used method to initialize an array in NumPy is np.repeat().
    • It creates a new array by making a specified number of copies of elements on each axis and placing them along the desired axis.
    • The stated axis can be no more than the original array’s dimension.

This method may be thought of as element-wise repeat, that is, if an array is a LEGO model, np.repeat() makes copies of each individual piece and assemble one set of copies before moving on to the next. On the other hand, if we want to make photocopies of the entire model and tile them up like in Python lists, we need to use np.tile() instead.

import numpy as np

data = np.random.randint(1, 9, (2, 3))
print(f'original array is {data}')

# np.repeat(an_array, repeats, axis)
repeated_data_0 = np.repeat(data, 2, axis=0)
print(f'array repeated along axis 0 is {repeated_data_0}')

repeated_data_1 = np.repeat(data, 2, axis=1)
print(f'array repeated along axis 1 is {repeated_data_1}')

'''
original array is [[5 4 6]
                   [2 4 5]]
array repeated along axis 0 is [[5 4 6]
                                [5 4 6]
                                [2 4 5]
                                [2 4 5]]
array repeated along axis 1 is [[5 5 4 4 6 6]
                                [2 2 4 4 5 5]]
'''

Indexing and Broadcasting

Array Indexing

Slicing 

arr[for_axis_0, for_axis_1, ...]

Slicing an array is similar to slicing a list. The main difference between the two is that we can slice an array based on our wanted axes. Let’s take a look at a few examples below.

import numpy as np

data = np.arange(1, 7).reshape((3,-1))
print(f'original data is {data}')

print(f'data at 0 on axis=0 and at 1 on axis=1 is {data[0, 1]}')

print(f'data from 1 to 3 on axis=0 is {data[1:3]}')

print(f'data from 0 to 2 on axis=0 and at 0 on axis=1 is {data[0:2, 0]}')

print(f'data from end to start on axis=0 and from start to end on axis=1 is {data[:, :]}')

'''
original data is [[1 2]
                  [3 4]
                  [5 6]]
data at 0 on axis=0 and at 1 on axis=1 is 2
data from 1 to 3 on axis=0 is [[3 4]
                               [5 6]]
data from 0 to 2 on axis=0 and at 0 on axis=1 is [1 3]
data from end to start on axis=0 and from start to end on axis=1 is [[5 6]
                                                                     [3 4]
                                                                     [1 2]]
'''

Using the idea of slicing or indexing, we can also update an array. Note that updating a slice of an array changes the original array and vice versa. Visually, slicing an array is like revealing one part of an image rather than making a copy of that part.

import numpy as np

data = np.arange(1, 7).reshape((2,-1))
print(f'original data is {data}')

slice_data = data[:, 1:]
slice_data[0, 0] = 100

print(f'data after updating slice is {data}')

'''
original data is [[1 2 3]
                  [4 5 6]]
data after updating slice is [[1 100 3]
                              [4   5 6]]
'''

Using Lists as Indices
Lists can only return an equally-spaced subset of its whereas we can extract random elements from an array using a list of its indices and the slicing syntax.

import numpy as np 

data = np.arange(1,7).reshape((2,-1))
print(f'original data is {data}')

sliced_data = data[[1],[0,2]]
print(f'data on the second row of axis=0 and at indices 0 and 2 of axis=1 is {sliced_data}')

'''
original data is [[1 2 3]
                  [4 5 6]]
data on the second row of axis=0 and at indices 0 and 2 of axis=1 is [4 6]
'''

Boolean Indices
Boolean indices is an efficent way of filtering data, referring to having a list of “True” or “False” as indices. This happens when we compare an array, technically its elements, to some value. NumPy then keeps only elements of index “True” and wrap them all in a 1D array.

import numpy as np 

data = np.arange(1,7).reshape((2,-1))
print(f'original data is {data}')

# test
boolean_idx = data > 2
print(f'boolean indices are {boolean_idx}')

result = data[boolean_idx]
print(f'elements of original data passing boolean indices is {result}')

'''
original data is [[1 2 3]
                  [4 5 6]]
boolean indices are [[False False True]
                     [True  True  True]]
elements of original data passing boolean indices is [3 4 5 6]
'''

print(f'summation along axis=0 is {np.sum(data, axis=0)}')
print(f'summation along axis=1 is {np.sum(data, axis=1)}')

'''

                  [4 5 6]]

summation along axis=0 is [5 7 9]
summation along axis=1 is [6 15]

Similar to summation, we can compute maximum or minimum values for an array as a whole or along specific axes using max() or min().

print(f'max values along axis=1 is {data.max(axis=1)}')

Broadcasting

Operations introduced in a moment do not change the original array. Matrix and Scalar
In Mathematics, we can multiply and divide a matrix by a scalar. We can do the same thing with an array in Python. Moreover, we can perform addition, subtraction, and exponential expression between a matrix and a scalar. This is a simple example of execution-implementation views mentioned at the beginning of this post.

import numpy as np

data = np.arange(1,7).reshape((2,-1))
print(f'original data is {data}')

# test
print(f'data multiplied by 2 is {data * 2}')
print(f'data adding 2 is {data + 2}')
print(f'data subtracted from 2 is {2 - data}')

'''

                  [4 5 6]]

                         [8 10 12]]
data adding 2 is [[3 4 5]
                  [6 7 8]]

Matrix and Vector
Instead of a scalar, NumPy allows basic mathematical operations between a matrix and a vector. In this case, a suitable vector is stretched to have the shape of the matrix and operations are carried out element-wise. In order for the extension to work, the shape of the vector must match the trailing dimensions of the matrix.

data = np.arange(24).reshape((2, 3, 4))
print(f'Original data is {data} and its shape is {data.shape}')

# 1D vector: shape (4,)
vector = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(f'Vector is {vector} and its shape is {vector.shape}')

# Add the vector to the 3D array
result = data + vector
print(f'A matrix added to a vector results in {result} and its shape is {result.shape}')

:bulb: Application in AI

AI is heavily applied to image data, especially in fields like computer vision and medical imaging. One of the basic AI applications is to change the brightness of images. Computers cannot interact with any other data but numerical one, thus we always have to convert images into a matrix of numeric values.

If you know the definition of function in Mathematics or still remember function in Python, conversion mimics such an idea—the domain/input contains 2D images and the range/ouptut contains multi-dimensional matrices depending on the kind of image input. Specifically, an image is an ndarray, but an ndarray is not necessarily represented by an image. We’ll discuss this more later.

An image can be measured by the number of pixels within itself or its height and width. We can compute the resolution of an image using these three parameters.

  • Grayscale images: 2D matrices (Height, Width) of scalar pixels $p$ such that $0 \le p \le 255$ with 0 for black and 255 for white.
  • RGB Color images: 3D matrices (Height, Width, channel) of matrix pixels \(p = \begin{bmatrix} r \\ g \\ b \end{bmatrix}\) where $0 \le r, g, b \le 255$. This convention comes straight from the field of art where primary color channels including red R, green G, and blue B when mixed can represent colors in images.

OpenCV

  1. OpenCV is to read, load, and save images. Image reading automatically performs the conversion.
  2. matplotlib is to load images read by OpenCV.

Here we only demonstrate using matplotlib to load images it works on both local and remote servers.

(162, 311, 3)

:question: Do you notice the difference in color between the original image and the one read by OpenCV and loaded by matplotlib? What do you think we can do to fix it?

This is a subtle but critical difference since color accuracy makes a tremendous impact on practical applications of vision and image-processing tasks, specifically in the field of AI.

  • Regular color image: channels are in order of R G B.
  • OpenCV color: images are read in order of B G R.
  • matplotlib color: images are saved and loaded in order of R G B.

Check out the following code and pictures to see this concept clearly when a red image becomes blue.

import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# create a pure red image (in BGR format for OpenCV)
red_bgr = np.zeros((162, 311, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
red_bgr[:, :] = [0, 0, 255]  # B=0, G=0, R=255 → Red

# save the image using OpenCV (optional)
cv2.imwrite('red_image.png', red_bgr)

# read the red image using OpenCV
img = cv2.imread('red_image.png')
print(img) # R=0, G=0, B=255 -> Blue

# display with matplotlib WITHOUT color conversion
plt.imshow(img)
plt.title('Should Be Red, But Looks Blue')
plt.axis('off')

Recall that an image is an ndarray which, up to this point, we know how to manipulate using NumPy techniques we’ve learned. For this specific array, (Height, Width, channel), we wish to keep the first two dimensions but modify the order of channel from RGB to BGR. We can also use a built-in method in OpenCV before loading the image with matplotlib.

Brightness Changes

Data Type
Earlier we said an image is an ndarray but an ndarray is not necessarily represented by an image. The reason behind is that their elements’ values are of different data types.

  • ndarray’s data type is int64 or float64.
  • images’ data type is uint8 representing 8 bits with unsigned/non-negative integers in from 0 to 255, particularly modulo 256—the values start back from 0 after 255.

Just like other data types in Python, we can always cast them to a specified type, which is exactly what we want since we want to make an array an image and vice versa.

a_variable.astype(np.a_data_type)

data = np.array([0.2, 255.6])
print('before changing data type')
print(data)
print(data.dtype)

data = data.astype(np.uint8)
print('after changing data type')
print(data)
print(data.dtype)

'''
before changing data type
[2.000e-01 2.556e+02]
float64
after changing data type
[  0 255]
uint8
'''

Naive Solution to Brightness Change - Issue with uint8
The property of modulo 256 is unit8’s own issue. If we want to brighten an image, a solution is to add some value to each elements of channels. But this causes light-colored regions become dark since modulo operates circularly rather than linearly.

grayscale_image = cv2.imread('M02W01Wed_numpy/4.opencv/image2.png', 0)

# attempt to make an image brighter
grayscale_image = grayscale_image + 50

Practial Solution to Brightness

  1. Step 1: To make an image data type linear, we can apply casting to force its data type to be float64 which can handle beyond 255 before addition.

     grayscale_image = grayscale_image.astype(float64)
 grayscale_image = grayscale + 100

  2. Limit the brightness for out-of-bound values using np.clip() or np.where().

     # np.clip(an_array, min_assigned_to_all_less_than, max_assigned_to_all_less_than)
 lighter_grayscale_image_clip = np.clip(grayscale_image, 0, 255)
 lighter_grayscale_image = lighter_grayscale_image_clip.astype(np.uint8)

     # np.where(condition, array_element_for_True, array_element_for_False)
 lighter_grayscale_image_where = np.where(lighter_grayscale_image > 255, 255, lighter_grayscale_image)
 lighter_grayscale_image = lighter_grayscale_image_where.astype(np.uint8)
